subtopic: PLUTONIUM-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SALE TO FRANCE

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PLUTONIUM-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SALE TO FRANCE
speechtext:
Officials of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and the French Commissariat a PEnergie Atomique have for some time been engaged in discussions in order to work out satisfactory arrangements for the sale to France of plutonium produced in the Canadian nuclear power reactors at Rolphton and Douglas Point, Ontario. These arrangements have been completed and have now been approved by both the government of France and the government of Canada.
The French Commissariat a l'Energie Atomique has undertaken intensive research in the development of plutonium burning, fast breeder, nuclear power reactors. Although France is able to fill some of her requirements for plutonium domestically, additional quantities are required in order not to delay the development program. Current Canadian programs, on the other hand, do not fully utilize the plutonium being produced in our reactors. Discussions between the French Commissariat and A.E.C.L. on the possible
supply of plutonium from Canada, therefore, came as a natural outcome of the collaboration between the two government agencies.
It is a long standing policy of the Canadian government that nuclear materials be exported from Canada for peaceful purposes only. With the full agreement of the French government it has been decided that the plutonium which will be used in the French civil nuclear program will be transferred to France under the provisions of the agreement between Canada and the European Atomic Energy Community, of which France is of course a member. This agreement provides for the application of EURATGM safeguards, and for procedures whereby Canada may obtain assurance that the Community's safeguards and control system is satisfactory and effective for any material transferred under the agreement from Canada to the member states of EUR ATOM. The role is fully compatible with Canada's signature of the test ban treaty and of the NPT.
I	should also like to point out that the agreement concluded between Canada and India in 1963 regarding the construction of a nuclear power station in Rajasthan, India, similar to the Douglas Point nuclear power station, provided for reciprocal bilateral safeguards on the Rajasthan and Douglas Point nuclear power stations and any special nuclear materials produced in them. The government of India has therefore been consulted regarding the safeguards arrangements to be applied on transfers to France of plutonium produced in the Douglas Point nuclear power station.
Mr. R. Gordon L. Fairweather (Fundy
Royal): The statement just made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs is interesting. It would be better, of course, if spokesmen for other parties had been given some warning so that useful comment could be made.
I am sure this party is delighted to know that emphasis has been placed on non-military use, and also that there is provision for full inspection. I hope France has been urged to sign the non-proliferation treaty.

Mr. Speaker, the situation in the Middle East is, of course, of very great concern to the Canadian government. Our position has been, and remains, that the best hope for a settlement in that area rests in resolution 242 of the Security Council and in the efforts of Ambassador Jarring to see that it is implemented by both sides. I have heard that the Israeli government is now proposing some immediate measures. These will certainly be looked upon sympathetically by the Canadian government, and we hope they will appeal to all sides so as to promote a settlement.
On the second question, the moving of the embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem, the Canadian government has not taken this step because the question of the future of Jerusalem has been a highly controversial one. Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a few words about the Biafran question. After hearing the Secretary of State for External Affairs waffle for several days about the unfortunate situation in Nigeria, we heard the Prime Minister on Friday make a clearcut statement. I welcome the Prime Minister's participation in this serious question but I suggest that his line of argument of Friday last had as its basis bad legal reasoning and an even worse morality.
From the first days of this session of parliament we have heard nothing but evasive answers from the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The minister says that our government does nothing to aid the Biafrans because the Biafran government objects to our using their one airstrip. The minister did not say that that airstrip could be used for the transport of military supplies as well as food; nor did he say that the Biafrans were prepared to build an alternate airstrip if we, in turn, were prepared to send in food and medical supplies.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Next we heard from the Secretary of State for External Affairs that the government was concerned about upsetting the feelings of the government of Nigeria. He suggested that the Nigerian government would be upset if Canada flew medical supplies and food to Biafra. Finally we heard the deplorable statement from the Prime Minister last Friday that any intervention by the government of Canada in the matter of Biafra would constitute an act of war against Nigeria. It seems to me we have gone all the way in the past ten days from evasive platitudes by the Secretary of State for External Affairs to a position of legal improbability and moral indifference on the part of the Prime Minister.
Let me say a couple of things on this point. First, it was by no means clear that if Canada, acting on its own as a nation, were to fly food and medical supplies into Biafra contrary to the wishes of Nigeria, we would be acting in an aggressive or warlike way toward Nigeria. The whole body of international law as it has developed since 1945 suggests that strictly from a legal point of
Interim Supply
view the Canadian government would be acting quite properly. The Canadian government could cite all kinds of precedents both in international law and in conventions passed by the United Nations to support its position. The United Nations convention against genocide, the United Nations statement on human rights, the legal precedent of the Nuremberg trials-all could be cited by the Canadian government in support of a decision to send food and medical supplies to the starving people of Biafra whether or not the government of Nigeria approved.
In saying this I am not suggesting that genocide is necessarily being practised in Nigeria. This would presuppose a deliberate policy on the part of the Nigerian government to murder a whole group of people, which is not being assumed by myself or by my hon. friends in the New Democratic party. But we do know that thousands of people are starving daily and we do know that from this point of view we could and should act. Surely this is all that is required. It is not necessary to presuppose that genocide is being committed. We do have good evidence from independent bodies all over the world that thousands are starving and this should surely be enough to justify us in going ahead.
Even in terms of international law Canada could present a good case, in my view, for going ahead and acting as a sovereign state. Of course, what many members of the house have suggested is that Canada should not act as a sovereign state but should act indirectly through the International Red Cross as Sweden has done. Does the Prime Minister, who comes here with his moral homilies about private behaviour and government behaviour, really suggest that the government of Nigeria would say that Canada, by bringing food and medical supplies to Biafra, was engaged in a belligerant, hostile and warlike action? Would Nigeria dare claim before the United Nations or any other international body that by bringing food and medical supplies to a group of starving people we were acting in a warlike manner? I suggest this is nonsense, and the government must know it is nonsense.
I placed a question before the Secretary of State for External Affairs a short while ago and received an answer to the effect that the Nigerian government has not suggested to the Canadian government that an action of the kind I am supporting in terms of providing food and medical supplies to the people of Biafra would be seen as an act of war. It would appear, therefore, that this is simply

September 30, 1968
Interim Supply
an assumption made by the Canadian government itself, or else it is a loosely worded, inflammatory statement made by the Prime Minister to avoid moral and political responsibility. Instead of helping starving people the Prime Minister has presented to the house an argument which I suggest is without legal foundation in terms of international law. At the very least, it can be thoroughly disputed in terms of international law. Yet he has presented this view as a self-evident truth which no reasonable and intelligent men should take for granted.
As I say, from a legal point of view it was probably an erroneous statement to start with. But beyond the question of legality lies the moral issue. I suggest that even if in terms of international law the position taken by the Canadian government in deciding to send supplies were seen to be incorrect, we do have nevertheless a moral responsibility when thousands of people are starving. The same thing happened in the thirties in Germany. Many governments at that time took the position that it was an internal matter; they did not want to upset relations with another government so they did not concern themselves. Are we to stand back now, at the end of the sixties, at a time when thousands of other people are starving and base our apology for lack of action on a dubious line of reasoning to the effect that we might be acting illegally? To me, this is a clear act of bad morality and something of which we in this house should be thoroughly ashamed.
I welcome the Prime Minister's decision to take part in a discussion of this question. He finally did have something to say to the house on this subject when he spoke on Friday. Unfortunately, what he had to say was illogical, misleading and morally offensive.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, just a few words at this stage of the debate on interim supply to refer to some assertions or insinuations made in this house last week, last Friday to be more precise, by a government member. I want to say that the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain), former mayor of his city, former independent member of parliament, stated in this house, after a referendum held in his riding, that 92 per cent of his electors preferred to see him remain an independent member rather than see him shift his political allegiance to any political party whatsoever.

Last Friday, referring to the spokesman of the Ralliement Creditiste, the member for Trois-Rivieres said:
The spokesman of the Ralliement Creditiste has of course referred again to the philosophy in which he believes-and I think he is sincere-but it does not seem practical to those who feel that one has to live within one's means.
The member for Trois-Rivieres was then speaking exactly like the ministers of the crown, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and the other members of the government party, today as well as in the past. In fact, when Conservatives were in office, they were saying exactly the same thing, that the Creditiste doctrine however good it may be is not practical, and that we must, indeed live within our means.
Mr. Chairman, in our opinion, the means at our disposal are those which allow us to develop our natural, intellectual and other ressources. We should adjust our finances to these possibilities instead of trying to adjust our development to our financial means. That is the realistic thing to do. We see and we face reality, while succeeding governments only see financial objections to the programs which could be undertaken in Canada.
If we ask ourselves: Can we build housing for those who need it; do we have wood; do we have nails; do we have bricks; do we have the materials necessary? In my opinion nobody knows the answer. Everybody without exception will answer: We have all that in Canada, but we do not have the money to put the materials together and to build houses for our people. And it is the same in all fields. There is an ever-growing need for universities, hospitals, schools, but it never occurs to a member to ask himself: Do we have contractors, engineers, talented men, people with a good head on their shoulders? Do we have materials to build hospitals and schools, or whatever we need? But we say at once like the member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain, who incidentally does not depart from the custom of the old parties, that we do not have the necessary money.
At present, Mr. Chairman, it is fantastic to see what is happening in Canada. Our municipalities kneel before the government, begging it not to discontinue winter works which helped municipalities during the difficult months of the year. To provinces which have to deal with great financial problems, the federal government says: Tighten your belt because we have no money either, no
September 30, 1968

credit, no financial means. We too have to cut expenditures, not because we do not need services, or we do not want to provide them, but because we do not have the means to financing them. That is the problem, but nobody is tackling it. On the contrary, we go on saying, like the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres, and I quote:
I know that our friends in the Ralliement Credi-tiste have a magic formula, and I would be the happiest man on earth if it were adopted.
However, he does everything he can not to understand it, and he keeps repeating that the formula is magic. The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres is certainly in the clouds, as all the others. If a war was declared to-morrow morning, I expect the hon. member for Manicouagan (Mr. Blouin) would also find it funny, but God knows that there are a good many destitute people on the North Coast.
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order.
Is this a point of order or a question?
Would the hon. member allow a question?
Certainly, Mr. Chairman.

If the hon. member for Temis-camingue reads further in Hansard, he will see that I too, last Wednesday, spoke about the notice of motion presented to the house by the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Peddle).

I take the word of the hon. member for Manicouagan, Mr. Chairman. I accuse him of nothing I simply quote certain facts. I tell him that the majority of the members in the old political parties who sat on the government side have always given the same answer, and the hon. member is aware that this government gives exactly the same answer as the previous one.
What I want to bring to the attention of the hon. member is the fact that in his riding as in mine, as in all the other ridings, we have to face the same problems which are not problems of production but problems of distribution of existing goods. The goods exist, if they did not, it would be different.
If we lived half a century ago, we would have to ask ourselves by what means a man could double or treble his production, or even increase it fivefold. But today this is not the case anymore. With automation, with the use of modern discoveries, science and machinery, the Canadian produces a hundred times
Interim Supply
more than he can consume and I have had, Mr. Chairman, a weeklong example of this. I happened to be a member of a delegation of French-speaking Canadian parliamentarians and to meet in Paris and Versailles Frenchspeaking parliamentarians from Africa, Europe and South America. We were able to witness each and everybody's problem while encountering people eager to reach arrangements and understandings as between members of the great French-speaking family. We are not against this; we are aware, however, .that their problems are not confined to the aspect of language but have also to do with economics. As for the black people of Africa we met, their sole desire is to enjoy the right to live in their homeland; they ask for nothing else.

Hear, hear.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)

In France, Quebec is often quoted as an example. They tell us: France is going to save you. Mr. Chairman, the contrary is far more probable, for Canada could perhaps help to save France.
During our stay in France, we learned that the Fiat Company is controlling today 30 per cent of Citroen, because the French did not have the necessary capital to save their own automobile industry.
Some tell us that France will save us financially. I studied the French standard of living. Please note that I am of French descent, but I am a Canadian, and if the two countries must be compared, let us not be shy about it. On the last evening of our visit we were invited to a formal banquet. There were men and women there who came from all parts of the world, or almost, and I had the opportunity of discussing with someone who is active in politics. But I was not content to attend that banquet only. I had the opportunity of visiting French workers, of seeing French farmers, their organization with regard to productivity, their means of distribution, of seeing what the standard of living of the French worker, of the French farmer is compared to that of his Canadian opposite.
Mr. Chairman, the difference is unbelievable. The salaries in France do not amount to even 50 per cent of the salary paid to our Canadian workers. The worker in France pays about 35 to 45 per cent more rent than a worker in Canada; and here, in Canada, how we complain about the rents being too high. You can imagine what the situation is like in France.

September 30, 1968
Interim Supply
I ask about the cost of a pound of butter and I am told it is $1.35 a pound. I am speaking about France, not about China, and their workers earn half as much as ours. To our question: How much does an automobile worker earn in the employ of Citroen or Renault? We get the reply: from $2,400 to $2,700 in Canadian dollars. It is higher.
And with regard to modern conveniences, they know nothing about it, absolutely nothing. I was staying at the Hotel Royal de Versailles. It is time-worn, it is old. They have not got around to installing toilets next to each bedroom: you have to go down the hall, as we used to do here in Canada 35 years ago. Their way of life is not at all like ours. They are perfectly happy with their traditions, and God knows there are many. We saw quite a number of castles dating from the reigns of Louis XIV and Louis XV, as well as huge and marvelous paintings, but this does not prevent the complaints of the individual dying of hunger. This is always something!
Mr. Chairman, meanwhile the farmers are stuck with their products. This is in France, not Africa. In Africa, the conditions are not any better, they are worse, Africans are asking France to help them. From the cultural point of view, I recognize that France has a part to play, but the Frenchman is mostly interested in economic matters.
In Africa, the same problem exists. A French-speaking priest from Madagascar told me that they had just received a gift from the United States:	three modern and wellequipped ambulances with drugs, lancets, and the like. They sent that to us in Madagascar, but imagine the difficulties we have encountered. They are too long for our roads and too wide for our streets, it takes the whole width of the street. We had to park the three ambulances in a field and it was hardly large enough for them. These are facts, Mr. Chairman. To turn in a Madagascar street, the ambulance would have to back up at least three times and go forward four times before being able to get around the street corner. It is not modern.
We must not bear a grudge against those people, but when we hear some people here clamouring that Canada is deprived of everything, it is false. However, Mr. Chairman, I do not mean that we must not try to correct abuses which do exist in Canada. This should not prevent us from seeing that a large number of our people lack the necessities of life.

On the whole, we have much greater opportunities here than in any of those countries, France included.
French culture is all well and good but if we have to go back 50 years, Mr. Chairman, we are not interested. Before going to France, I did not mind too much hearing "Frenchmen of Canada". But when I came back, last night, I much preferred to hear "French Canadians". It might mean the same thing, but I am not prepared to say so.
We are happy to be Canadians and in spite of everything we hear, the delegates from other countries respected us when they knew we were from Canada. There were only six Canadian parliamentarians and we were treated like kings with great tactfulness.
We noticed on the spot that their problems are still unsolved. Before trying to solve ours, they should deal with their own because that will keep them busy for a hundred years. For at least a hundred years, because there has been little change in a great many years.
All that, Mr. Chairman, to say that I have been asserting for the last 25 years that we live in the country with the greatest potential in the world. Our country has more natural resources than the United States. However, we must consider the fact that modern technology and evolution nevertheless originated in the United States which, no matter what people say elsewhere in the world, have rendered tremendous services.
We had the occasion, for instance-I mention that in passing-of speaking of satellites to extend the French-speaking community or enable citizens in French-speaking countries to see one another on television. But the technical facilities in all those countries are next to nothing while the United States controls 95 per cent of the facilities already in operation. Whether it is in English or in French does not matter, the technical possibilities belong to the United States.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Even if we wanted it to be otherwise, and in some areas Canadians are stirred up against United States, we should realize-as shown by facts-that our standard of living is closely related to that of the Americans. However, this does not mean that we should let ourselves be exploited or crushed. No. But let us begin by understanding that what we have, we have not created by ourselves; that we have been helped on our continent, not by Africa, not by China or Russia, but by a country on our continent. And before making wild gestures against our neighbours, let us
September 30, 19G8

start by watching what goes on in other countries oi the world, and then we will become realistic.
Mr. Chairman, we all wish to become fully independent and have a maximum of sovereignty. This is everybody's wish. This is each individual's wish, whether he comes from a family of 10, 15 or 20 children. Each one wishes to attain his own individual freedom and his own individual sovereignty. Whether he is a businessman, a professional, or a farmer, or whether he is working in another areas of the Canadian economy, each individual wishes to be respected and not to receive orders from anybody.
We are all individually and collectively in the same situation. We wish to be a sovereign nation. Unfortunately, there is a impediment preventing Canada from becoming sovereign. The impediment is of a financial nature. It is not because there is a shortage of intelligent people. Not at all. It is purely and definitely financial, but every government has managed to overcome that financial impediment or hindrance for war purposes. If a war were to break out tomorrow morning, no minister would rise to say: Unfortunately, we cannot participate in the war effort because we have no money. On the contrary, all of them would introduce a motion providing for the adoption of the necessary estimates in order to set up war industries and to set the whole system in motion. Nothing would be lacking, of course not. We would be told, this is an emergency.
Emergencies exist in peacetime just like in wartime. When Canadian mothers wonder what to give to their children the next day, it is essential for a responsible government to assume its responsibilities. It is urgent for a government composed of human beings, blessed with intelligence, to see through those fictitious impediments created by those who control the economic blood of the nation, those who control our money and credit are the real leaders of the country, those who grant permissions. But people like the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) do not see that.
The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres continued and I quote:
I excuse most of my friends-
-he was talking about the Creditistes-
-for I believe them to be sincere, but, in my opinion, it is to mislead people who are uninformed-
Imagine if this is an intelligent remark. The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres is no doubt
Interim Supply
well informed, and this is why he sits on the last benches of the Liberal party. We can be sure that he will stay there for a long time. I am convinced of this-because puppets never get very far in this world. To be a good backbencher you always have to stand up and fight. I continue my quotation:
-to make people who are uninformed believe that these things could happen thanks to a magic wand which would reform the entire system is to mislead them.
Why talk about a magic wand? There is no question of a magic wand. It is simply a question of passing legislation like any other which we have already passed. Let us pass legislation in order to suppress poverty in Canada-call it what you want-but it will be legislation which will make everyone reasonably well off.
This does not mean that everybody will be rich or a millionaire, but it does mean that every Canadian will at least be assured of a decent standard of living, of a minimum of comfort. He will be assured of having three meals a day, decent clothes, decent housing, medical care when necessary and of getting the education that is available and must be accessible to all. That is the vital minimum, a decent standard of living. Once that is provided, let competition and private initiative be free. If someone has enough initiative to build up a good business or to run an important industry, let him be free to do so, but at least let all the people without exception be assured a decent standard of living. We do not need a magic wand to bring this about, merely a law which will guarantee a decent standard of living.
The Prime Minister told us the other day: We have no money. However, he did not tell us that we have no schools, that we have no clothes, that we have no hospitals, that we have no doctors, that we have no professionals, that we have no different social classes, for he knows that we do have them. He did not tell us that all the stores in Canada are overstocked with goods, that not a single one of them has run out of goods because manufacturers have quit producing them. Nor did he tell us that the farmers had quit producing. No. We are even stuck with agricultural produce, with wheat, and in our own provinces stuck with our fruit and vegetables. Why? Because we cannot sell them. The Prime Minister did not say there was a shortage of those things.
He told us: For a lack of money, we are forced to discontinue those services, we are forced to discontinue winter works programs,

September 30, 1968
Interim Supply
we will be forced this fall to study with the provinces the possibility of decreasing social welfare to those who are totally destitute. We are forced to. By whom? By finance, by the financial system.
And at the same time, we are told through the interim supply bill that the interest alone on the national debt of Canada will cost this year, without taking into account the interests the provinces, municipalities, school boards, and individuals will pay, one billion and a half. The Prime Minister did not say: We will ask the financiers to wait ten years before we start paying them premiums or interest. No, that is sacred, we have no right to touch that.
In fact, the total interest this year amounts to $200 million more than what we paid last year. Two hundred million dollars! This is just peanuts according to the government. It is possible that Canadians are overtaxed to provide for the paying of interests to capitalists, that cursed race devouring Canada. We are caught in those conditions, but nobody considers introducing some legislation. We hear about a magic wand to change conditions.
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to dwell on that matter. I simply wish to tell you how much some hon. members, such as the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres, are oil the beam and that they are precisely those who prevent the passage of federal legislation which could guarantee decent means of living to which I referred earlier to all Canadian citizens.
Mr. Chairman, I believe that the consideration of the supply motion provides a good opportunity to emphasize and clearly state what is suggested by the Creditistes when they say: To make financially possible what is physically possible. Not create endless, unlimited credit, but according to what we can physically do. Newspapers will not say a word about that.
They are not there.

They are not there; anyway, there is no one in the gallery. They are there when the time comes to attack the Ralliement Creditiste or Social Credit, or to say: The Creditistes repeat themselves. To my knowledge, newspapers have been repeating themselves by flattering the Liberals, then the Conservatives, for about 35 years. Nothing changes, but we do not worry about it. They did not give us our seats in parliament and they will not turn us out either.

However, we shall make every effort to have accepted the system we suggest, that is to make financially possible what is both physically possible and desirable for the people of Canada. It is as simple as that. It is not a question of a machine which will print endless dollars, it is a question of making credit available on the basis of the rate of production of the Canadian people. It is an economic system, an accounting system. It is Pius XI- and not I-who said in 1931, 37 years ago already: Economics will only reach its objectives when it will make available to everybody-not only to the Liberals, not only to the Conservatives, not only to the members of the N.D.P., but to everyone-a part of the goods that God's nature and men's industry can produce, and such a share ought to be large enough to provide for each and every one at least a decent living. This was said 37 years ago. StiU, up to now, the point has not been understood. Delegates and ministers are sent in Europe, and everywhere else. They are supposed to find world markets for the export of our current products, of Canada's production next year, and so forth. Ministers are sent to inquire from our own nationals and find out what they need. In our opinion, the first demand that should be satisfied is on the Canadian market. Now, let us first meet the requirements of that market. Afterwards, we might send ministers to France and other European countries, to Africa, Japan, China, the North Pole and the South Pole, and dispose of our excess products. But in the meantime, Mr. Chairman, I wish the government would take its responsibilities and give us a system that will help us satisfy the needs of each and every Canadian citizen.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, the leader of the Ralliement Creditiste spoke eloquently of the opportunity to help peoples in other parts of the world. I agree with him that we are happy to live here in Canada, where conditions can be changed and improved. I also agree with him in recognizing that we must work now to bring about the necessary changes and improvements, and that is why I want to speak of Canada this afternoon.

Hear, hear.

I
feel that the Canadian people as a whole are very much disposed to give this new government a full chance to show what it can do,
September 30, 1968



knowing that it is the first government for a long time to be in a majority position, although some of us felt that the former government had a de facto majority. However, this time there is no doubt on the point. Therefore I believe that most Canadians are saying: Now that they are there for the first time with a big majority, let us see what they can do.
We are all in accord with the objective of the government in trying to streamline parliament and become more efficient in the ways in which we do things here. We are not going to be in accord if it comes to the point where the opposition will be silenced or restricted in bringing to the attention of the government the conditions in this country and the needs of our people. We, too, have suffered from the old-fashioned methods of carrying out the business of parliament and we are thoroughly in agreement that we need a greater modernization and streamlining of our parliamentary procedures. However, Mr. Chairman, I think there is a real danger that in streamlining the procedures of parliament the government may be inclined to take for granted that it can talk in terms of getting ready and proceeding to explore programs and policies for future years, and does not have to do anything in the immediate present to look after the needs of the people of this country. I would point out that those needs are very great at this time.
In short, I am afraid the government may be throwing out the baby with the bath water because people, tolerant as a great many people in our constituencies have been, are worried about certain moves which have already been made in respect of the needs of Canadians. I refer to the cutting off of the winter works program. I refer to the fact that we have been told there will be no increase in family allowances this session in spite of the rise in the cost of living. I refer to the fact that we have been told there will be no increase in the basic old age security pension even though the cost of living has risen tremendously.
I refer to the casual reply given today in connection with veterans legislation. I know such long range programs will take time but I feel there will be a terrible interim between now and subsequent sessions when, if these programs are not improved, people will continue to suffer hardship. People like ourselves, who are reasonably well off, know nothing about the hardship these people will 29180-37

have to endure. We do not know what it feels like to live from pay cheque to pay cheque. We do not know what it feels like to be mortgaged to the hilt as a great many people are, even people fairly well off relative to the poverty line, in order to get all the things that modern advertising tells us are "musts" if we are to live like modern human beings. We do not know what it is like to suddenly have an increase in the cost of living, or to find oneself or one's family stricken with illness, or in one way or another to have the pay cheque removed. I am afraid this government does not realize that there are in our country people for whom the just society cannot be put off until next year, the year after that or the year after that, that the beginnings of the just society must be made manifest in a great many more concrete ways this session. It is all very well to say that we cannot afford these things. However, I looked at the estimates the other day and saw that a very nice, big chunk of money, $27,246,000, had been allocated for a medical research council. I am not quarrelling with that, although I would like to know more about how this money will be spent. But I also note that in the estimates there is no similar allocation to start a human research council to carry out research into the conditions under which people in this country live and to which the leader of the Creditistes just referred.
It seems to me that so far in our deliberations in this house one thing has been almost overlooked. I refer to a brand new point in the report of the Economic Council of Canada. This feature of the report has been highlighted in the press. It was again highlighted in the Toronto Globe and Mail today. I refer to the poverty that exists in this country, poverty which we condone as the headline in the Toronto newspaper says. It is pointed out how very low the minimum wages in this country are relative to the needs of families living under today's conditions.
Evidence is mountain high that conditions in this beautiful, rich country of Canada, as we heard it described this afternoon, are far from what they must be if we are to develop the full potential of our population. We know that half our population, the lower income half, is living in varying degrees of insecurity and frustration. We know that one Canadian in five is living in poverty. I suggest to hon. members that when half of the population is living in varying degrees of insecurity and

September 30, 1968

frustration we have an unstable, unsatisfactory situation with regard to which the government must take action. Even if the government's majority were twice as large, if it does not take action it is heading for trouble, in capital letters, because people will not stay indefinitely in such a condition.
I think there is still some misunderstanding, certainly in some government offices, about the modern meaning of the word "poverty". In order to do away with any misunderstanding on this point. I quote the definition given recently by the Economic Council of Canada. I do so because I do not think it has been brought home sufficiently. It is as follows:
To feel poverty is, among other things, to feel oneself an unwilling outsider-a virtual non-participant in the society in which one lives. The problem of poverty in developed industrial societies is increasingly viewed, not as a sheer lack of essentials to sustain life, but as an insufficient access to certain goods, services, and conditions of life which are available to everyone else and have come to be accepted as basic to a decent, minimum standard of living.
The economic council is at pains to point out that poverty is relative. This means that even if conditions in Canada are much better than those in Africa, France or anywhere else, conditions here are not, relatively speaking, much better because in Canada the difference between poverty and affluence is very great. People in this country who are poor can see others with wealth, affluence, comfort and security, to which they themselves have no access.
We in this group have worked very hard over the years to have measures of social security passed to close that gap. But I point out that we have today reached the stage where social security measures necessary and indeed essential as they are, are no longer enough. We have to go beyond social security. In a society where no one has a modern car, no one is poor because he does not have a car. However, in our society the great majority of people have cars. This means of transportation has become the accepted way of life and those without cars are regarded as substandard people living in substandard conditions.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
It is all very well to talk about the dignity of poverty. There is no dignity in poverty and no status in poverty and we should not be thinking in terms of more handouts here and there and more social security here and there.
[Mrs. Maclnnis (Vancouver-Kingsway) .1
This is not enough, necessary as it is. We have to give people access to those things which will make modern living possible for them.
Old age pension, family allowance and unemployment insurance measures have been enacted as well as measures during wartime to control the prices of goods and services. Again I agree with the leader of the Credi-tiste party that if during a war in an emergency something can be done to control the cost of living, this same action can be taken in an emergency in peacetime. If half the population suffers from some degree of insecurity and frustration and one-fifth of the population is in poverty, how many more people have to be in such a state before it is considered an emergency? There is an emergency now for 20 per cent of Canadian families who do not have the basic things they need.
We have enacted measures to help the provinces with various social security programs. Now we have medicare. I was glad to hear the announcement over the week end that on April 1 Manitoba will also join the federal medicare program together with Nova Scotia, British Columbia and Saskatchewan. I have been prophesying for a long time that the old age pension story would be repeated all over again and that after the first province joined the others would dribble in one after the other, as they did with the old age pensions program, and it will not take nine years for them to do so in this case. The Prime Minister said with reference to medicare, "we have had enough of that free stuff", but the people of Canada have got to the stage where they are determined to live in a modem way.
Whether the government likes it or not, it is now deeply involved in the problem of ensuring that modern housing is provided for those who cannot afford it themselves. It is true that the Minister of Transport may now be riding off in all directions at once as did Don Quixote on his horse, Rosinante, with a task force which I believe is now creaking a bit in the joints. But all the same the government will find out that a task force on housing will not bring the horse to the stable. She will also have to be fed and looked after properly because the people want housing and want it badly.
When we find several cabinet ministers as well as the Leader of the Opposition advocating a guaranteed annual income, we can see that the pressures for social change are mounting fast in this country. These pressures are greatest in our big cities. I think
September 30, 1968

that the problems of the cities must be dealt with in a big way and must be dealt with now. We should not wait until we have the just society in a blueprint to deal with the problems in big cities.
Some hon. members may have seen the article in the Montreal Star of September 19, 1968 quoting Adolph A. Berle Jr. It said:
In a recent issue of Saturday Review, Mr. Berle launched an attack on the facade of the gross national product-that annual figure which politicians and economists love to cite as reflecting a nation's economic health. All the GNP tells us, Mr. Berle contends, is how much money is expended in any given year for goods and services. What it does not tell us is what he calls the gross national disproduct: the toll taken on a society by garbage, waste, air and water pollution, violence, vandalism, malnutrition, disease, deaths and injuries caused by motor vehicles, respiratory ailments related to consumption of tobacco-
Where is the hon. member for Surrey?
-and so on.
Until those things are also computed and subtracted from the GNP to arrive at true net national product (not as that term is used at present), we will not have an accurate picture of our society and its needs, says Mr. Berle. It is a refreshing theory and one that does not deserve to be brushed off, as it already has been by some economists. Their sole job, they argue, is to compute, not philosophize or indulge in value judgments; they have no way of determining what is "good" or "bad".
It is because we need so badly an accurate picture of our society and its needs that I would seriously urge an item in the estimates for a human research council. I submit that there is another reason for it apart from building a quality society-and how I was taken to task for that term when I referred to it last year in the committees. I think we badly need a quality society. I submit there is another reason why this government, beside building a quality society, should undertake human research with special emphasis on urban dislocations and urban problems.
If the government is to spend the taxpayers' money wisely and if it is to cut out waste and unnecessary spending, we must have an accurate picture of today's society and its needs. If we are to have a just or even a sane society, we will have to look hard at certain areas in our population. We will have to be prepared to spend money on them so that we can cut expenditures in other areas.
I wonder whether we have any idea of the cost of poor housing across this country. I wonder whether any estimate has been made of how much taxpayers' money is going into 29180-371
Interim Supply
the cost of physical and mental illness, delinquency and crime, family breakdown, divorce and all the other social ills which stem from bad housing. I think there is a scandalous waste of the taxpayers' money in these directions. To say simply that municipal, provincial or federal money will be spent on them is no answer, because John Q. Public and Jane Q. Public have to pay the bill whether it is spent through the federal, provincial or municipal authority.
Today we are spending millions of dollars of the taxpayers' hard-earned money on completely unnecessary expenditures which arise from bad conditions owing to bad housing, bad town planning and bad environmental conditions for our people. The same thing is true of pollution. We are just beginning now to realize the vast amounts of taxation which will be needed to cope with pollution if we allow it to continue. Pollution of water, air and soil and noise pollution all exact their toll not only in terms of human well-being but in terms of wealth production and in terms of having to pay hard-earned taxes to try to clean up the mess. Neglecting pollution means a scandalous waste of taxpayers' dollars.
Then we come to the people themselves, the waste of our human resources both from the standpoint of our own development and the development of the wealth production of this country. Thousands of people now on social assistance could and should be converted from social outcasts into self-respecting citizens and taxpayers.
I have been through the public housing developments in my own and in adjoining ridings and I know there are men and women there eating their hearts out because they are obliged to live on social assistance with its stigma of public charity when they know perfectly well that if they could get the necessary training for the kind of work they could do they would be able to hold up their heads with pride and contribute their share to the wealth of Canada instead of having to sit there and take handouts. These people are not down and out, except that they are shut out of our way of life; they are shut out of the community of life that the rest of us share. Research into human problems could aid enormously in developing a process for getting these people off social assistance and on to the taxpayers' rolls.

and the old ways of governments, to realize that we are in 1968 and that a new century is just around the corner.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE-PROCEDURES RESPECTING INSTRUMENTS IN VIRTUE OF STATUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion which has now been called was being debated on Wednesday, September 25. A number of members had spoken and I believe I had the floor when debate was interrupted. Before continuing with my remarks I express the hope that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) might be asked to come into the house-if this is one of the days he is allowed to come-because I regard this as a matter of considerable importance.
I was talking last Wednesday and propose to continue talking about a particular order in council which was passed on April 25 of this year by the present government. I refer to this order in council because it shows, in an outstanding way, the need for the kind of committee we are proposing to establish, a
578	COMMONS
Consideration of Procedural Changes committee to consider ways and means of reviewing legislation that is enacted by bodies to which we delegate certain authority.
As was indicated in speeches last Wednesday, quite a few boards, commissions and other bodies are given authority to enact legislation. I wish to refer to one particular body, namely the cabinet itself. I think the committee to be established by this motion ought to take a pretty good look at the way in which the cabinet exercises authority under orders in council to enact legislation, and some way ought to be established of reviewing this practice.
The particular example I referred to last Wednesday bears mentioning again. By way of background I reminded hon. members that in June, 1962, the Conservative government of the day passed an order in council which had the effect of raising import duties. It is generally understood, I think, that the law of the land is that only parliament may impose taxation. The Conservative government in 1962, just after the election of June 18, found a novel and ingenious way of raising taxes by order in council. They did it in a one-two way.
Initially they raised taxes by a considerable amount under a section in the Customs Tariff. Then they reduced those taxes to the level they wanted to achieve by using section 22 of the Financial Administration Act, which gives the Governor in Council power to remit any tax if the Governor in Council feels that it is in the public interest to do so.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I will not go into all the whys and wherefores of the 1962 story but I repeat with emphasis that the Liberals of the day attacked this action bitterly and vigorously. One after another, led by Hon. Paul Martin who was in the front row and supported by the present Minister of Justice who was in the back row, they stood up and denounced what had happened. We were in the fight, too, but the main point of my story is that the Liberals contended that this action by order in council was invalid and illegal. Both they and we tried to get the government of that day to give us the opinion from the Department of Justice upon the basis of which it had been decided that this order in council was valid. The government refused. Hon. Paul Martin had a motion on the order paper seeking to have this opinion tabled. We debated it at length; it was talked out, of course, under the rules of that day. We could

DEBATES	September 30, 1968
not get what we wanted. The point is that the Liberals made a stand on that occasion. Here was the government using section 22 of the Financial Administration Act for a purpose for which it was not intended. They took the same position when they were the government by getting parliament to pass a bill validating the order in council to which objection had been taken, thus confirming that in their view it was invalid unless passed, or approved, by parliament.
Now, Mr. Speaker, these same people are back in power-I realize there are some new faces, but they belong to the same party. And they are now resorting to the very trick which they condemned out of hand when the Conservatives practised it in 1962. This time the Liberals found they wanted to change the customs law. I agree there is a slight difference of direction. The Conservatives wanted to put certain import duties up; the Liberals wanted to bring them down. The Liberals placed the appropriate motions on the order paper of the last parliament preparatory to doing this very thing. They were put on the order paper on June 1, 1967, and on November 6, 1967. But they were never passed, because parliament was dissolved before we got round to them. However, the fact that these resolutions were on the order paper clearly indicates that the government knew that the way to get the customs law changed was to get parliament to change it. But they did not get the law changed. Parliament was dissolved on April 23 and two days later, on April 25, the Liberal government of the present Prime Minister passed order in council PC1968/816 which relies on the same section 22 of the Financial Administration Act which they said in 1962 could not be used for this purpose.
This is somewhat technical, but I think the actual terms of this order in council should be on the record, so I shall read its operative sections:
1,	This order may be cited as the Customs Tariff Remission Order, 1968.
2.	Remission is hereby granted in respect of all goods imported or taken out of warehouse for consumption on or after April 24, 1968, and all goods previously imported for which no entry for consumption was made before that date, of that part of the customs duty and sales tax payable thereon under the Customs Tariff and the Excise Tax Act equal to the amount by which
(a)	the customs duty and sales tax payable thereon exceeds
(b)	the amount of the customs duty and sales tax that would have been payable thereon if legislation had been enacted before the date of this Order based upon the resolutions relating to the Customs Tariff tabled in the House of Commons on June 1, 1967, and November 6, 1967.
September 30, 1968	COMMONS
I have read the entire operative part of the order in council. It says, in the plainest of language, something like this: By order in council we have brought in the law which parliament did not pass because it was dissolved before it could deal with certain resolutions which were on the order paper. Well, if this is not doing precisely the same thing as the Conservative government did in 1962 I do not understand the meaning of words.
The difference is, of course, that in 1962 the Conservatives used this device to raise import duties. There were companies and interests in this country which did not like this, and they were taking the government to court. In the present instance the import duties were reduced, so nobody is taking the government to court. But is this the touchstone of our political morality? Is this the basis upon which to use the power given by order in council-you use it when you can get away with it and you do not use it when you cannot get away with it? I think this is just as clear a violation of the proper use of these powers as that which was condemned so roundly by the Liberals in 1962.
I asked the Minister of Justice a question about this issue some days ago during the orders of the day question period. I asked him whether all aspects of it had been checked, especially bearing in mind the previous decision by the Department of Justice, before approval was given to the order. All I got by way of answer was the one word "yes". I am afraid I do not have a great deal of confidence in these opinions from a Department of Justice which can rule one way in 1962, the opposite way in 1963, then back again in 1968.
I shall not take the time to put the whole text of section 22 of the Financial Administration Act on the record. I read it again today, and it is clear to me that it is not the kind of provision which is to be used in a general way for reducing a tax for doing away with something which parliament has enacted. I believe this misuse of orders in council needs to be examined very carefully, and this is one of the reasons I am supporting the motion which is now before us, in the hope we can be given an opportunity to look into this kind of thing.
As a matter of fact, I suspect there have been a number of occasions upon which this power has been misused. I have another order in my hand-P.C. 1968-832, passed on April 30, 1968. It has to do with investment in the Churchill Falls Labrador Corporation,
DEBATES	579
Consideration of Procedural Changes popularly known as Brinco. This is a long order and I do not intend to read it all. But again it is a question of the government drafting an order in council which relies on section 22 of the Financial Administration Act.
The government decides that it wants to exempt from taxation investment in American dollars in a certain development, namely, Brinco. The law is there. The law says such investment is subject to taxation. But the government simply declares that under section 22 of the Financial Administration Act these taxes are to be remitted-they need not be paid because a decision has been made by order in council.

Mr. Speaker, as an introduction to my remarks on this motion I would like to refer briefly to the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) speech to this house at the opening of this session. First, I would like to say I agree with much of what he had to say as recorded at page 73 of Hansard for September 16. As a Canadian I can say I hope his remarks were sincere, which will prove me wrong in my former interpretation of his political philosophy. I hope his words were not just mere window dressing because I wish to commend him for some of his remarks, but because of his actions since that occasion at the opening of the house I have now developed some reservations.
On that occasion the Prime Minister said, as recorded on page 72 of Hansard:
It is the government's function to propose legislative solutions. It is the opposition's task to question these solutions and attempt to improve them or propose alternatives.
We hope that the government will accept some of the alternatives that we have proposed and that we intend to propose. We are not opposed to change in our parliamentary rules, as some people in this house and in the press seem to think, provided freedom of speech is maintained. The Prime Minister went on to say:
Neither role can be subordinate to the other. It goes without saying that any proposal for procedural reform must assist both sides of this house to function more efficiently. Anything less would be self-defeating. Anything less would diminish the very institution which we seek to assist. The discussions which have been proceeding on and off for the past fortnight, or even longer, among the representatives of the several parties in the house must not be permitted to continue indefinitely.
Our house leader, the hon, member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), has stated that this party is willing to co-operate. He has stated that time and time again both in this house and outside it. But he has also said we
[Mr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) .1
will not capitulate. I hope that the government understands our position in this regard.
The Prime Minister went on to say:
Nor should they be permitted to lead, either by agreement or in the absence of it, to procedural changes which will upset the delicate and essential balance between government and opposition so necessary to the proper functioning of parliament.
In regard to the proper functioning of parliament I say that with proper co-operation from both sides parliament will function, but co-operation actually is a two-way street. As I said before, it does not mean that the opposition will capitulate. I hope that the Prime Minister meant what he said. He went on to add:
Good legislation, effective legislation, requires the expenditure of extensive effort on both sides of this house.
We agree with that. He also said:
It is our responsibility as members to engage here in discussions which are as knowledgeable as possible.
But, Mr. Speaker, we as members of this house have many other responsibilities. We as private members have responsibilities that are possibly a little different from the responsibilities of members of the government, and I wish to refer to one or two of our responsibilities.
I would like to remind the Prime Minister that it is our responsibility, as members of the opposition, to see that the government does not always impose its will on parliament, and by "parliament" in this context I mean the people of Canada. It is also our responsibility as elected members of this house to see that freedom of speech is maintained. I think this is the foremost responsibility of backbenchers on this side of the house. However, it is also the responsibility of the government to see that freedom of speech is maintained.
It is also our responsibility as elected members to be accountable to the citizens of Canada for any authority that we delegate to other agencies, and that is what this resolution is about. It is also our responsibility to right some of the injustices we have inflicted upon the public by reason of authority delegated by members of parliament. It is also our responsibility to see that our democratic system of government is upheld and maintained, and that is one of the reasons that I am speaking on this resolution today.
