speechtext:
Then I shall get down to the point in the Prime Minister's speech which deals with the resolution. At page 73 of Hansard he said:
A possible change, for example, but one which must be examined carefully, is the practice of delegating legislative authority, in terms of ministerial orders and orders made in council, and in the sense of decisions of quasi-judicial bodies. Whatever we decide, it should be based on a full knowledge of both the strengths and the weaknesses of our present practices.
I should like to deal mainly with the weaknesses of our present practices in respect of delegated legislative authority. This is very important. In my opinion the discussion on this resolution is long overdue. In my opinion it deals with one of the most important, most neglected and even one of the most dangerous aspects of the present method of governing our country.
We are, at last, opening the door on the question of the use of the delegated powers of parliament. This is a very large and formidable question that has created problems which, if not solved now, could eventually lead to our complete impotence as a governing body. If any member believes I exaggerate, let me simply refer him to the vast body of writing on the subject that already exists. Let the doubters search their own correspondence which they have had with their constituents, read the daily press and recall their own personal dealings with any one of the hundreds of government agencies. I am sure they will then agree that every day in this country there are hundreds of instances, some of insignificance, some of great importance, where the rights of citizens have been encroached upon by the unbridled use of power by public servants.
No one in this house is more eager than I to deal thoroughly and quickly with this resolution. My interest in the question is of long standing. It dates, in fact, from the day more than ten years ago when as a freshman member of parliament I suddenly became shockingly aware of the power of and the abuse of power by our national bureaucracy. This bureaucracy is not composed simply of the host of civil servants who man the ministerial departments of government. It includes the army of those who staff the crown corporations, the boards, the agencies, the commissions and regulatory bodies that have sprung
September 30, 1968

Consideration of Procedural Changes up like weeds as the business of governing the nation has become increasingly complex and difficult.
Let me hasten to say that the problem of the exercise of power and the misuse of power delegated to an unwieldy and largely autonomous bureaucracy is not peculiar to Canada. It affects all countries with a democratic form of government and, I suspect, even those countries which subscribe to monolithic and authoritarian forms of government. Many of these countries have attacked the problem over a long period with varying success. I know of none who believe they have found a complete answer. But it is my hope that by dealing intelligently with this resolution we will be taking a giant step toward our own satisfactory solution.
I have said that my concern with the question is of long standing. In 1962 I was concerned enough with the many examples of arbitrary and unjust use of power by bureaucrats at all levels to introduce a private member's bill seeking to establish some control over bureaucratic oppression. This bill came forward for debate as Bill C-39 of 1963. It was in the form of an amendment to the Civil Service Act. It would have made it an offence for "any person holding an office, commission or employment, temporary or permanent, in the service of the government of Canada, at the nomination of the crown or at the nomination of any of the officers of the government of Canada" to "deprive or attempt to deprive a person of any right or freedom recognized and declared in the Canadian Bill of Rights." My aim at that time was set out in the explanatory notes to the bill:
-to ensure the application of the Canadian Bill of Rights to the multitudinous and ever-multiplying federal statutes, rules, orders, regulations, bylaws and proclamations; to the end that the citizen may go in peace about his lawful occasions free of wrongful harassment in legal guise by holders of public office. The bill gives the Canadian citizen a voice to warn and a rod to chasten those of his servants who, in	pride of	the	power	he	hasentrusted to them,	corruptly	pervert his	laws	tohis own hurt; to crown servants it gives the Canadian Bill of	Rights as	the	golden	rule	bywhich to measure	the rights	and	freedoms of	the
citizen-
Perhaps that was not the right method by which to achieve my aim. Perhaps the time was not ripe. The fact is, however, that the problem was pressing then and is even more so today, six years of legislation later. My aim remains the same. However, this time there appears to be more chance of achievement. As everyone knows, a private member's bill has scant chance of becoming law.

Its fate is usually to be talked out as was mine. The measure before us today is a government resolution backed not only by the stature of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Drury) but the prestige of the Prime Minister whose remarks on the subject both inside and outside this house have left little doubt that he is in agreement with taking some steps to curb official licence. It has the further advantage, I am led to understand, of approval in general terms by all parties in the house.
It is true that the resolution as it stands is nothing more than an expression to set up a special committee to consider the problem of what might be contrived to enable this house to effectively police the powers parliament has already delegated or may in future delegate to various branches of the public service under statute. But I believe it is to be an historic start. It is my hope that the discussion of the need to adopt the resolution will go a long way toward helping the deliberations of any committee that may subsequently be set up and toward enabling this house to meet adequately the vital question of controlling the arbitrary exercise of power by the bureaucracy. I can think of no more urgent problem facing the twenty eighth parliament. We all are familiar with the chorus of criticism in recent years of parliament and parliamentarians. I think much of the criticism is exaggerated and misplaced. But we cannot very well blame our critics for confusing government, as seen through the activities of parliament, with government as experienced by the average citizen when faced with parliament's administrative apparatus, the bureaucracy.
Most critics, when their charges are examined, are found to have had a brush with the uncontrolled and unsupervised use of delegated authority and not with parliament. They have been understandably unable to distinguish in such cases between those in parliament who create the instrument of power and those outside parliament who anonymously wield that power. In my opinion this has been largely our own fault and the fault of our colleagues in previous parliaments. There has been a failure on the part of members to attach conditions and safeguards to the transfer of responsibility and power. Too often they have lightly passed on the responsibilities placed upon their shoulders by the fact of their election to parliament to appointed officials who are not subject to the harsh accounting of public opinion. Too often we
September 30, 1968

have given power without ensuring that those to whom power is delegated will exercise it unselfishly and with impartial justice.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
If there is a bureaucratic tyranny, if there is bureaucratic oppression, if there is periodic abuse of trust granted in good faith, and I for one believe there is, then it is we in parliament who are to blame. By adopting this resolution and endorsing the course of action it envisages I believe we can go a long way toward making restitution.
We can no longer slough off our responsibilities on others or give unrestricted grants of vast power with the attitude of "let George do it". If there is one thing we are charged with as members of parliament it is to ensure equal justice to all Canadians and to protect the rights and liberties of the individual and the rights and liberties of minorities.
There is no more deadly enemy of the democratic form of government, no more secret and sinister threat to our free way of life, than the arbitrary exercise of power beyond the forms and processes of ordinary law by hordes of anonymous officials.
By electing us to parliament, the people of Canada have placed in our hands tremendous power. If we transfer this power to others and fail to ensure that it is not used to victimize those who gave us this trust, then we are derelict in our duty and we will have opened wide the door to dictatorship by bureaucracy and we will have betrayed our cherished heritage of individual liberty and democratic government.
We are being asked to set up a committee that will study the problem of enabling the house to review instruments made in virtue of any statute of the parliament of Canada, that is to say, a committee that will recommend the establishment of some agency or procedure and some means of allowing parliament to make accountable to parliament those who exercise power in its name. I think this is a timely resolution and very appropriate.
If such a committee is set up I believe it is important that there be a clear understanding beforehand of what is expected of it. It is important that its members know exactly what this house wishes it to do, what general line it is expected to pursue and something of the dimensions and importance of the problems that it will be asked to consider.
First, let it be clearly understood that there is nothing essentially wrong about the delegation of authority. I believe this to be an 29180-38J
Consideration of Procedural Changes essential operation of modem government. Without delegation of power and authority government today, complex and fantastically detailed and growing more so every day, would scarcely be possible. Without such a device we would face a complete breakdown of government administration, chaos and anarchy.
It is not the delegation of power and authority which is dangerous, it is rather the imperfect manner in which, up to now, it has been done. We have been careless and irresponsible in the use of what should be an essential and effective tool of government. Professor Harold J. Laski was not among the many constitutional authorities in Great Britain who decried delegated authority and the increase in so-called administrative law. He did not agree that it was a dangerous trend which should be stamped out. In his "Parliamentary Government in England" he described the delegated power as:
-an elementary procedural convenience essential to the positive state.
Having said that he warned:
The vital thing is that parliament should be in a position to make objection to any use of it when it deems fit, and that it should be so able to examine what is done in its name as to make it certain that nothing to which objection can be taken escapes from its purview.
In other words, he says to use the device but to take sensible precautions. This sums up, I think, in my view what the resolution now before us seeks to do.
The question that will most closely concern any committee that may be set up as a consequence of our adopting this resolution will be the means whereby parliament will always be in a position to keep delegated power and authority within its purview. I feel sure there will be many who will immediately think of the old idea of an ombudsman. It is a theory that I favoured for a long time. But surely setting up an ombudsman would merely be establishing another government official. When we consider the scant regard paid by the executive to our present economic watchdog, the Auditor General, we realize how ineffective this would be. Besides, appointing another official outside parliament to do a job that is clearly that of members of parliament would be begging the suggestion that this was just another abdication of responsibility. We must not abdicate our responsibilities as members of parliament as has been done in the past.
In the experience of some countries, most notably and most recently the United Kingdom, the office of ombudsman appears to
September 30, 1968

Consideration of Procedural Changes have degenerated into a general complaint bureau or, alternatively, into a futile bit of window dressing for the democratic process. What we need, I believe, is a parliamentary body that will be armed with power to call witnesses and for the production of papers without regard to governmental rank or influence, and that will be empowered to pursue its own course free of direction or influence by the government. It must be strong enough and free enough to ride close herd on all recipients of parliament's delegated authority and to command their compliance and respect.
The pattern of the public accounts committee of this house with its chairman drawn from the opposition ranks might be a very good one to follow. To me the essential features must be that its findings, reports and recommendations must carry with them some compulsion on the executive or individually responsible members of the executive, the Prime Minister and cabinet ministers, to take subsequent action. The very least that must be done is to ensure that anything turned up by the watchdog group gets a fair and public hearing in this group.
I believe the relationship of the cabinet to any such body will dictate its success and also its failure. Let us never forget, when we consider the untrammeled exercise of power by the bureaucracy, that the executive, in light of recent parliamentary history, must be placed at the head of any list of those to be scrutinized. It would be my hope that any method that may be developed for overseeing the indiscriminate use of power would consider as a priority item the use of that executive device we know, as referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), as the order in council.
I would like to recall to members the words of a committee of the Canadian Bar Association as quoted in the Montreal Gazette on November 11:
Under democratic institutions the people expect to be governed, but on condition that the laws should be discussed in the open, traversed by the criticism of the opposition and be the result of free and enlightened decision by parliament.
There is no governmental device more murky and less open than the order in council.
Having suggested some of the forms which the proposed body might take and some of the lines along which I believe it should operate, I should like to warn against some of the things it should not be and some of the things it should not be allowed to do. There is

always a grave danger that what appears on the surface so fair and so promising can be perverted into something menacing and tyrannous. Such measures as are encompassed within the resolution before us can be looked at in two ways, viewed from the front or the rear according to the person who is looking with a purpose.
What I am seeking to warn against is this house establishing one type of thing and finding later on it is being used quite differently. A parliamentary body, ostensibly intended to police misuse of delegated power, could equally well be utilized by a skilful and cynical executive to cover up wrongdoing. An unscrupulous and dictatorial executive could turn it into an instrument for preventing exposure of anything embarrassing to it, for burying aggravating disclosures, delaying remedial action and for scattering dust in the public eye. Anyone who has any experience with parliamentary committees will realize just what I mean. In fact, mention was made of this the other night by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) when he referred to the use of the committees system. The use of a government majority and a government chairman to stifle discussion and frustrate action is not unknown. The embalming of a committee's findings by the simple expedient of tabling is not unknown. I realize that in many statements inside and outside the house the Prime Minister has endorsed the theory of parliament controlling the growing power of bureaucracy. I was reassured to find traces of this sentiment in the speech from the throne and more specific endorsa-tion, as I said when I started my speech, when he spoke on leaders' day in the house.
s (5:30 p.m.)
I also noticed in the speech from the throne mention of a plan to centralize all government information services in order to better inform Canadians about their government and bring individual Canadians closer to their government. This is a very estimable aim, a laudable endeavour if indeed those things are the end result. But just suppose that for one of many possible reasons the Prime Minister is not able personally to direct such bold new enterprises as the centralized information service and the enterprise envisaged in this resolution; suppose the initiative in these matters falls to others, particularly into the sphere of the advice and influence of senior civil servants. Both projects could change in the twinkling of an eye from
September 30, 1968

necessary and effective projects to dangerous props of arbitrary government.
I hope members opposite will forgive me for mentioning such an unlikely possibility as a Liberal government seeking to perpetuate itself in office, but I do so only to illustrate the care that must be taken in establishing any agency of parliament to carry out such a delicate and provocative task as policing delegated powers.
I have not attempted at this time, Mr. Speaker, to deal at any great length with the background and development of the problem of delegated authority, delegated powers, administrative law and related topics. There is already a vast amount of literature on the subject. I am taking it for granted that everyone here is at least aware that the problem exists and is urgent. It is a reality of our times in regard to government, but it is by no means new. The first world war, with its tremendous burdens upon government, its compounding of government responsibilities, accentuated something that had already existed for a long time. In 1929 the government of Great Britain studied it and took measures to control it. These measures are still operating today, however narrowly and faultily their critics may think.
In the same year the Lord Chief Justice of England, the right hon. Lord Hewart of Bury, described it as "the new despotism" in a book that has become a classic text on the subject. As early as that day he wrote:
A little inquiry will serve to show that there is now, and for some years past has been, a persistent influence at work which, whatever the motives or intentions that support it may be thought to be, undoubtedly has the effect of placing a large and increasing field of departmental authority and activity beyond the reach of the ordinary law.
He was concerned about parliament relinquishing its powers in the interest of expediency or apathy, to the detriment of our rights and liberties. On this he wrote:
Much toil, and not a little blood, have been spent in bringing slowly into being a policy wherein the people make the laws, and independent judges administer them. If that edifice is to be overthrown, let the overthrow be accomplished openly.
Never let it be said that liberty and justice having with difficulty been won, were suffered to be abstracted or impaired in a fit of absence of mind.
As members, we have all had experience at one time or another of misuse by public servants of power delegated to them by us and exercised by them against their fellow
Consideration of Procedural Changes citizens. I do not say that this is always deliberate, always calculated, always vicious. Sometimes it is mere bumbling, but bumbling the consequences of which can too often be escaped because there is no accounting. We should remember that delegated authority is wielded in the vast majority of cases by nameless, faceless bureaucrats who feel completely secure from retribution, hidden as they are in the maze of the public service jungle. Most abuses take place out of the public eye. I feel that publicity therefore is one of the chief weapons against abuse of power. I doubt if any department, including the Privy Council, any board, commission or other agency of government fails to contribute its daily mite to the staggering annual total of injustices done by government to its citizens.
It would serve little purpose at this point, Mr. Speaker, to cite individual cases. I am sure all of us could provide enough of these to take many sitting days and swamp Hansard. My files, in any case, are full of instances of bureaucratic injustice, and at a later time I will speak of some of them.
To my mind the worst aspect of the whole problem of the abuse of delegated power lies not with the actions of ordinary, middle-run civil servants but with the top brass of the public service and the opportunity it gives them to become a real threat to our chosen system of parliamentary democracy. I believe it is with them and their exercise of powers, especially in view of their position of tremendous influence and persuasion on ministers, that any parliamentary supervisory effort should be chiefly concerned.
I have said on other occasions in this house, and I should like to repeat it, that it matters not what party is in power and forms the government, it is really the power elite of the public service that runs the country. The government of the day is a captive of the top civil service brass; ministers are only hostages, completely dominated and directed by their top departmental officials.
This dominance is exerted by virtue, partly, of experience but principally through the power delegated to the appointed officials by statute. It is vital to oversee the use of this power if we are to maintain even the figment of elected government governing. As for the ordinary member of parliament, if the senior civil servant does not disregard us as being such small change as to be beneath his notice, he treats us like children who must be disciplined and never indulged. If any of you who
586	COMMONS
Consideration of Procedural Changes have been to departments have not yet found this out, you will do so in the next few weeks or months. I am talking from experience.
On this point I would like to quote what James Harvey and Katherine Hood have to say in their book, "The British State":
-delegated authority amounts to virtually uncontrolled making of laws by government .departments, and demonstrates the immense powers wielded by the senior permanent officials of the civil service.
They say further:
The cabinet would never be able to sustain the "dictatorship" which it nowadays exercises over the House of Commons without the indispensable assistance of the permanent civil service.
Later they say:
___a highly effective conspiracy of silence surrounds the activity of the civil service.

As my colleague the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) has just said, and the cabinet. Judging from the remarks of the Prime Minister in the past two or three weeks, there may in future be even more than we have been used to. I believe it is high time this silence was broken, that light was allowed into the dark places of the civil service power structure, and senior departmental officials were compelled to answer publicly and openly for the discharge of the trust handed them by parliament. If we set up a committee as suggested in this resolution, if that committee functions the way we want and expect it to function, it will give us this open criticism. We as members of parliament will be responsible for the power we have delegated. I think that is our main responsibility. I think this is one of the first responsibilities we should consider in this twenty eighth parliament, that we are responsible for delegated authority.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Writing of the implications of administrative justice, that handmaiden of delegated authority, N. C. Hinton in his "Government and the Citizen" noted:
The implications of this type of justice hardly need underlining. The citizen loses the benefit of the traditional impartiality of the courts. His rights may be adversely affected if they run contrary to government policy. Administrative decisions may fly in the face of true justice and logic.
I believe it is our duty in considering the purpose of this resolution to ensure that our citizens are provided with some means whereby parliament can protect them from

DEBATES	September 30, 1968
administrative abuse and injustice. I repeat that anything we do along this line must be effective and meaningful to ordinary Canadians, in other words, to our constituents. It cannot be mere camouflage, and I hope that the Prime Minister was not giving us just window dressing. I hope he was sincere in what he said. If we fail in this, we will have done a grave disservice to our people and our country.
I have never advocated that the practice of delegating authority be discontinued or even curtailed. All that is needed is supervision of its use. It can be an exceedingly valuable tool of government if properly handled. This is an opportunity to make it really effective. Let us cease the old practice of giving some anonymous group of appointed officials a blank cheque except for our signature with every piece of legislation we approve, which in fact is what we have been doing.
As some new members in the house may find out, the regulations are actually more powerful than some of the acts of parliament. I have found that out in individual cases. In other words, under our present system we have delegated our authority to these civil servants, and we have done so indiscriminately and with no responsibility. We cannot afford any longer to hand out so casually our power of attorney as members of parliament. Power to govern is our responsibility. Let us assume it fully by making sure that what is done in our name is done fairly, openly and with justice for all.
My early experience with the monster of bureaucracy wielding unregulated power has compelled me to fight it over the years. I am happy to take part in another such battle, as you well know, Mr. Speaker. Let me conclude by cautioning that in my view there is no surer way of poisoning parliamentary democracy than by abdicating our power without supervision of its use.

Mr. Speaker, in his speech, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) bemoaned the fact that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) had replied too briefly to his question of September 17 in which he outlined a similarity of methods and tactics between the Conservative government of 1962 and the Liberal government of 1967.
The hon. member recalled that, in 1962, the Conservative government had levied a new
September 30, 1968	COMMONS
tax through an order in council, whereas in 1967 a Liberal government had reimbursed taxes also through an order in council.

SUGGESTED INTEREST FREE LOANS TO UNIVERSITY STUDENTS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of introducing a measure which would allow loans to university students to be made interest free.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on August 21 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) announced that during the 1967-68 lending year, loans were made to 90,371 students. The total amount was $57,053,410. The government has estimated there will be a total of some 100,000 loans to students in the 1968-69 year, in a total amount of some $60 million. Since the act came into effect in 1964, 132,000 students have received loans totalling $160,900,000.
In his August 21 announcement the minister also gave the revised criteria for loan applications with regard to students independent of parental financial supervision. Formerly, such students were required to have completed three years post-secondary studies or be employed one year or be married. The new criteria demand four years of post-secondary studies, one year's employment and an age level of 21 years or marriage. The new criteria have been protested by the students union at the University of Saskatchewan. Student loans are interest free until six months after graduation at which time students start paying back and at which time interest at the rate of 5 J per cent is applied. Up to then, interest is paid by the government to the banks since student loans are government guaranteed bank loans.
Under the new formula proposed this summer, interest rates applied to loans taken out in the 1968-69 academic year will go from an estimated 7f per cent to 8 per cent, adding from $1.5 million to $2 million to student repayments. The argument is advanced that
September 30, 1968

the government should pay the total interest and make the loans interest free to students who in the year after graduation are faced with pyramiding costs of getting established in a profession and paying off multitudinous debts of which student loans are only a part.
Speaking in parliament on June 21, 1966, the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) suggested a number of improvements to the student loan program, including reciprocity between the Quebec and national plans as well as a remission of debt for students achieving a certain level of scholastic excellence. At that time the minister stated he looked to the day when tuition fees would be eliminated. One would hope the government at this time would take to heart the recommendations he made then from the freewheeling position of a minister without portfolio, prior to assuming the cares of office associated with the senior cabinet position he now holds.
Certainly, if the government cannot see its way clear to accept the advice of the present Minister of Justice and remove tuition fees completely through remission of loan payments to outstanding students, at least it could move at this point to remit interest rates after as well as before graduation, since the amount involved is minuscule in the light of the government's total requirements but nevertheless could be very significant to the individual student.
The point raised by the present Minister of Justice in 1966, relating to the dovetailing of the Quebec and Ottawa plans, was certainly well taken and was evidence of his appreciation of the divisive nature of the two student loan plans, one for Quebec and one for Ottawa. Regrettably, no advances have as yet been made permitting total reciprocity between the two plans. It is to be hoped that in his present responsible position he will again speak out in the cabinet council in favour of a national Canadian plan, thus permitting students from every province to study in any other province rather than the present divisive and restrictve program introduced by the Pearson government.
The total of student loans in Alberta in 1967-68 came to $6.4 million for some 10,500 students; in Saskatchewan, $5.9 million for some 7,300 students Manitoba, $3.2 million for some 4,600 students. Thus, on the prairie provinces the student loan program is of vital importance. There is no question in so far as students across Canada are concerned that the loans should be interest free, and rather than
Student Loans
increasing the interest rate in the current academic year the government should undertake to remove completely from the shoulders of students the accumulative burden of high interest payments. Generally speaking, it is students from low income families who most require loans. It goes without saying that such students should be encouraged in every way to attain the maximum development of their potential.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
From the economic viewpoint expenditures on education cannot be considered expenses; rather, they are investments. The more highly educated a student becomes the greater become his earning potential and productivity. He therefore pays increased income tax and in the long run the state benefits.
A few days ago I talked with some students from a nearby university and it soon became apparent that students of slender financial means felt society had discriminated against them. Through no fault of their own they had to live in squalid conditions in inferior quality housing and be faced with the prospect of a large debt on graduation. Now that debt carries considerable interest. Their feelings of being treated unfairly become stronger when they saw fellow students from well to do families living a life of relative financial ease, through no increased effort on their own part and not being faced with a large debt to pay after graduation.
By and large, Canadian students are a responsible and dedicated group of Canadians. In no country in the world does education play so important a role in the development of a nation as in Canada. This is an added reason for the necessity of accepting a greater degree of governmental involvement in education. Above all, it is necessary to foster closer relationship between secondary educational institutions in Quebec and those in the rest of Canada.
For too long we have had education going one way in one province and another way in another province. Surely, Mr. Speaker, since we all have the same staggering responsibilities in every province for the development and consolidation of this nation from coast to coast, we ought to move heaven and earth to improve and co-ordinate relations between students and educators, and between those in the general education movement in Quebec and educators in the other provinces.

September 30, 1968

Nothing could be or is more dangerous to the future freedom, independence and prosperity of this nation than the separation and compartmentalization of its secondary educational systems. Make no mistake, Mr. Speaker, Canada's future as a free and independent nation today is trembling in the balance. We all know how difficult it will be for Canada to survive in freedom against the tremendous social, economic and political pulls of the United States and Europe. It will be difficult for this country to remain united under the present circumstances. How much more difficult would our survival be if our country became a conglomeration of petty principalities.
We all know how much freedom and liberal thought exists in those areas of the world where nations are divided and national boundaries have stimulated generations of hatred. That sort of thing must not be our fate. That must not be the fate of our continental destiny.
Our education must be more in tune with the needs of the nation. It must be at a modern pace and use the tools of the electronic age rather than at the leisurely pace of 50 years ago. We must have education in depth. Education must be available to all who can utilize it, be they French, English or members of those other races and cultures whose presence has added a new dimension to the power of Canada. In this connection I cannot do better than refer to remarks made recently by a former member of the government, hon. Robert Winters, president of Brazilian Light and Power. Speaking in Windsor, Ontario, on September 21, Mr. Winters said:
To bring such facilities and faculties to all who have the wish and the ability to use them is a financial undertaking of the first magnitude. It requires the resources of all levels of government and the private sector.
He also said:
The level of education and the standard of national economic well-being are interrelated. In our case, it is the major reason for the shortfall in our economic performance compared with our better educated neighbours to the south.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, education cannot be geared exclusively to economic performance. It must be related to advancement in the entire field of human knowledge-science, economics, literature, the arts and so on.
Unquestionably, since Canada's population as it relates to national development is smaller than a similar sort of population in most
[Mr. Yewchuk.l
other countries, we must derive the utmost benefit from our educational system so that each Canadian may make a maximum contribution to the national advancement. There was a time when education was largely a matter of self-improvement. Today education affects the progress of our country, the mutual understanding among its citizens, the unity and development of the nation and the scientific, social and political evolution of our times. For this reason the federal government must share a greater part of the burden, not only with the provinces but also with the students.
It has been said that it is easy to suggest programs that entail the spending of government money; but it is another thing to determine from where money to pay for such programs is to come. I know that those who will speak against this idea will say to hon. members in the opposition, "I thought you wanted the government to save money and here you are, asking for more money to be spent. You cannot have it both ways." The field of education, I submit, ought to have priority over a great many other fields. At this time it might be well for the government to reassess some of its programs and determine whether all or part of the money being spent in those programs is being spent to the best advantage. One program which comes to mind is an across the board handout to our entire family population, namely, the family allowance program.
I ask the government to consider one question at this time when it is short of money and is considering its priorities. Do families with a taxable income of $10,000 or more annually really need a family allowance? Do such families need this little handout which was inaugurated many years ago when economic conditions were so vastly different? That program could be reassessed, keeping in mind national priorities and spending money in areas of greatest need. Personally, if other sources of funds can not be found, I think education is important enough to warrant a little increase in taxation.
Recent changes in federal participation have resulted in federal contributions to capital and operating costs of universities being increased to approximately 50 per cent. At the same time very little has been done to ease the burden on students. It is illusory for those in the government to think that saddling a student with a large financial obligation which must be repaid shortly after
September 30. 1968

graduation is in any way a gift to the student. It is not. The debt makes it possible for the student to graduate. Then, when all his resources are needed to enable him to become established, he is faced with a large debt which he must repay.
If Canada is to keep pace with the advances made in the United States and elsewhere in the world in medicine, space, science, aeronautics and so on, and not be hopelessly left behind in the expansion of knowledge, nothing is more urgent at this time than assistance to our students. As a small beginning, I urge a total remission of student loan interest charges.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I congratulate the mover of the motion. I agree with many of his points but I must say at the beginning of my remarks that though I support his motion my heart really is not in it. I feel that we must view education from the standpoint of Canada's place internationally and from the standpoint of its effects on our own population.
A couple of weeks ago the government was severely criticized for scrapping its winter works program. The government said that the winter works program was done away with because it was inadequate. Personally, I consider the student loan program totally inadequate. When the government thought its winter works program was wanting, so to speak, that program was scrapped forthwith. I know that we heard many vague mutterings on the subject of winter works. Nevertheless, a number of programs were suggested to take its place.
Today we are considering a reduction of loans and not the complete elimination of any particular grants. Perhaps we might consider this matter along the lines we considered the winter works program, if that is not taking our line of reasoning too far out of the way.
I do not think, as I said, that the Canada student loan program goes far enough. The house may recall that the inception of the program lay in some campaign promises in the 1963 federal election. We heard a good deal from the Liberals about 10,000 student scholarships. When the promise was transformed into legislation in 1964, as if by magic it became the Canada student loan plan.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
This plan has indeed helped to put thousands of students through university. It has also placed thousands of students in debt six months after their graduation. What we need today in this country is a greatly expanded
accessibility of education for students. Too few students go on to receive higher education; 16.9 per cent is the most recent figure I have heard, compared with well over 40 per cent in the United States. I think we have to consider education as being a right, not a privilege. Education should be considered as a means of enriching the human resources of our country, not only for the production of saleable skills but in the cultural aspects. The good life has to mean more than the ever-increasing consumption of goods. Accessibility means that regardless of income worthy students need travel allowances, better housing, far more in the way of educational and classroom facilities, much more by way of health facilities, books, supplies of various kinds. Our country is wealthy enough to provide a great deal more aid to students in all these directions-selfishly,	if you like,
because we depend on these students to provide the leadership in our society in the future.
There is a sociological side to accessibility. Even if we were to make university education completely free tomorrow it would take some sections of our society years to catch up with what this really means in terms of human betterment. I am thinking of the chronically unemployed, the chronically underprivileged, those who have checked out of our society and who do not understand that the way to a better life is through better education. So we must do more than provide free university education. We must set up a whole program along the lines of Headstart, a program which must be comprehensive and embrace our whole system of education. Only by such action can we put Canadians on an equal footing with students in some of the eastern countries and even in some countries of the west.
For too long we have depended upon the importation of skills. It seems to me there is something a little immoral about sending Canadian agents abroad to steal, if you like, the talent they find there, to drain the brains of other nations and make good the deficiencies that we have failed to overcome in our own. I am thinking of teachers, doctors, nurses; they are most welcome and we cannot do without them. But generally speaking they come from countries with a lower standard of living than our own which need the services of these people even more than we do. Their presence here indicates that we have failed to

Another 80,000 took technical or vocational training of one sort or another, thereby improving their employment potential and enhancing their contribution to the Canadian economy.
If the Canadian economy and the Canadian government's position are going to be enhanced by students going to university, then the government should do everything possible to assist them to do just that. It should not institute measures that are regressive. In my view the raising of the interest rate on student loans by 2 per cent is a regressive measure.
In this house we hear daily that we are in the midst of an inflationary spiral, and we also know that throughout the past summer many students had extreme difficulty in finding summer employment. If students are unable to earn money during the summer it follows that they will be more interested in borrowing money for their education. They should be assisted as much as possible when they go to borrow money from government sources, if it is the government's intention that they should do so, and I am not prepared to say I agree with that intention if it puts students deeper in debt.
The affluent can go to school quite easily. There is no problem there. Our problem in Canada is to broaden the educational base so that more of our young people can go to post-secondary institutions. I myself was most favoured to go with two of my high school classmates to university. My parents had the financial means to send me to university. However, there were a great many others of my age who had the ability to absorb university education but they did not have the means to attend university. I have always felt that others would have benefited equally, or perhaps to a greater degree, from the experience that I received by chance. Our job is to arrange our assistance so that it is no longer due to chance or accident of birth that students can go to university. The opportunity to go to university should be based on a student's ability to learn and not on his ability to pay.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I wish to comment briefly on the ceiling imposed on student loans. The $1,000 ceiling really goes only two-thirds of the way toward meeting the cost of a student's year at college. I myself have a daughter at school, and most people estimate that a student living away from home is faced with a charge of some $1,500 per year for the various costs associated with going to university.

This motion, Mr. Speaker, is a step in the right direction but it is only a timid step. We support it, knowing its imperfections. He is a worker without any income and therefore must be helped. Then the government very imaginatively thought of offering non-existent jobs. I was one of those students a few years ago. Mr. Speaker although it may be strange, in some areas I find myself in agreement with the comments made by the members of the opposition. I feel, however, that to some extent we are going after a gnat with a shotgun. I do not believe the significant question is whether the young men or young women who have been through university do or do not pay interest on their student loans. I think we are attacking the problem from the wrong end. It would seem to me that it should be of far greater concern to us whether the young men and women in our society who have the ability also have the opportunity to go to university. Once they have been there and have graduated they are in a much better position to repay these obligations than are the individuals in our society who never have had the opportunity to attend university.
I have some interesting figures published by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics for the
September 30, 1968

year 1966. If one receives an elementary education during his lifetime he can expect to earn $131,000. One who receives up to three years of secondary school education can expect to earn $168,000. One who receives four or five years of secondary education can expect to earn $209,000. The university graduate on the other hand can expect to earn over his working life an average of $350,000. This is almost three times what the men and women without an elementary education will earn and about 50 per cent or 75 per cent greater than the individual who has had secondary school education. Therefore I do not believe the problem regarding those who have completed university education and who are now out in the the labour market is really as significant a problem as that regarding those young men and women who should be attending our universities and are not.
I believe all education-and here I share the opinion of some members opposite- should be free for all. This basic human right should be available to all to enable them to achieve their fullest development. This is a right which must not be restricted in any way by accident of birth, economics or geography. The right to education at every level should be free and within the reach of all who have the ability. This should be a guaranteed right to everyone without equivocation. There still are many Canadians who could and should be attending university but who are not.
It is interesting to note that a survey by the Canadian Union of Students found that 25 per cent of our university students are from the homes of wage earners who are in the top 6 per cent bracket. I am prepared to grant that much more than purely matters of finance are involved. There is the question of motivation. Reference has been made to the Headstart program and other programs which might be of assistance to students in the younger age group.
I still believe that the lack of financial resources unquestionably prevents many young men and women attending university. I believe also that we should be looking at the matter of some form of subsidy for the young men and women who live beyond the commuting distance of a university. It is much easier for someone who has the good fortune to live in a university town to attend university than it is for someone who lives 250 or 300 miles away. I am not concerned as much with those people who have gone to university and are now working as I am with the others who should be going to university and
Student Loans
who for one reason or another have not been given the opportunity to do so.
My friend in the New Democratic party must be using some figures which are different from mine. It is my understanding that approximately 23 per cent of all Canadians in the 18 to 23 age group are attending post secondary education facilities whereas the figure on the other side of the border is double that, 46 per cent. I grant that there may be some variation in this because someone might argue that in some areas our education is superior, while in others perhaps it is not. In our modern economic and social structure it is absolutely vital that we do not waste the resources of our young men and women. I feel this is the most vital resource we possess and that we must do everything in our capacity to capitalize on it.
Earlier I mentioned fees. It is my understanding that fees now account for less than 15 per cent of the operating revenues received by universities. Therefore, in that context, the malarkey we often hear of a person having worked his way through university really is not true. He may have provided 15 per cent of the cost, but the other 85 per cent of the cost is borne by the taxpayers at large. I believe that to set this up as a barrier to prevent men and women attending university, who should be there, is absolutely wrong.
I would like to make one additional observation. The government is already spending substantial amounts of money on post secondary education. The members of the opposition the other day berated the government for its fiscal irresponsibility. I do not think that at any time since I became interested in this subject, and I have been in university work for a long time, have I seen a greater indication in these affluent times of difficulty on the part of individual students in meeting the basic needs of their university education.
While it may be said that of course this motion does not deal in toto with this immense problem, it is one practical and useful suggestion which falls within the purview of the legislature to which we belong. Certainly it would be very thoughtless of us if in what-the hon. member calls this electronic age we missed any opportunity in our search for education in depth for all. If we miss any opportunity to further the purpose which would appear to be in the minds of all who have spoken today, and the views which they hold so sincerely, it would be thoughtless.
Like one of the hon. members who has spoken, I have memories of going through that exercise which, in the archaic language of yesterday, we used to describe as working one's way through college. Some people recommend this as a recipe for all their successers. I have no patience with such a point of view. I think of the many opportunities to advance one's knowledge which are denied to young men or young women who

by economic necessity are forced to devote a part of their time to the hard, grim task of keeping body and soul together as they tread the halls of learning.
I welcome this suggestion of the hon. member. It is a very good one, and I think it is timely because, in spite of our affluence, I do believe there is a crisis in this very area of education. Hon. members in other parts of the house have pointed out documentation in respect of this very matter. We hardly need tell ourselves that the human resource is the one we dare not fail to develop to its fullest. If we compare what is going on in other countries we have no reason to be complacent.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose) stated very simply-this has been said before and it should never be forgotten- that it is the ability to learn and not the ability to pay which should be the criterion. There is a wastage of human resources and I am sure that this very day there are young Canadians who are not at university because of financial reasons. I agree also with those who have pointed out that the $1,000 figure is now unrealistic. I agree too with what they have said about the interest rate. I am appalled at the number of students who have applied for loans as they now exist, and have been turned down. There is disappointment among youth. I suppose somewhere all across Canada there are 50,000 young people who are disappointed because they did not receive these $1,000 scholarships that were promised in 1963 at the rate of $10,000 per year. But I would say, as in all of these things, that we must deal not in the past and drink the sour wine of unfulfilled promises, but urge, and I am sure the hon. member had this in mind, that in all the planning this government may do, and in all its efforts to mobilize our resources we surely must begin with those resources the hon. member had in mind as he constructed this interesting, valuable and helpful notice of motion. I say again how much I appreciate his initiative and his thoughtfulness in dealing with this subject, one demanding great priority.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on this notice of motion introduced by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) and asking that the government should study the possibility of removing the interest rate on loans to students.
September 30, 1968

The students loan program was put into effect in 1964 and I think it has helped many students already. Since 1964, 132,000 students have taken part in the program and approximately $160 million have been loaned by banks and guaranteed by the federal government.
I was fortunate enough to take part in that program because barely a few years ago I was a student. I can say that the program was welcomed with much enthusiasm by the students; they appreciated it and I think that it was at the time and still is a priority for the federal as well as the provincial governments.
On August 21 last, the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) explained that new administrative principles had been followed mainly so that only the students who really needed the program could participate therein. To that purpose, the administrative principles had been studied by the federal government and the provinces participating in that scheme, and by the Yukon and Northwest Territories.
I think that when the government considers the possibilities of implementing a program and spending more money on a certain program, it must determine which one of the two would be of greater use to the country. Whether it is directly paid by the federal government, or under an agreement with the provincial governments, it is very important to decide.
I would like to point out to the house that there are still areas in this country where primary schools do not have the necessary facilities to give pupils as good an education as elsewhere in the country. The same is true for high schools, and I can give you an example. There is a lack of physical education facilities in many places, and I think especially of my own province, New Brunswick. In my opinion, there is a priority at the secondary level. There is also a gap in the development of a physical education program.
The hon. member for Athabaska now suggests a measure of assistance for the students. He and other hon. members have spoken of helping the students. I completely agree. I think that we should seriously consider the possibility of helping anyone who wants to study., only in that case let us help the students. A student who graduates is no longer a student.
Student Loans
For example, in the last academic year, between July 1, 1967 and June 30, 1968, about $57 million were lent to 90,371 students. At the interest rate of that time, which was 5J per cent, that amounts to about $3 million. The hon. members of the opposition agree that we must have priorities and that we must help the students. They ask us to give $3 million to students who have graduated and who have entered a profession, who are now lawyers, chartered accountants or professors, and to forget about the other programs. In my opinion, priority should really be given to students in secondary schools, in primary schools and in university. We should give priority to those groups that really need it.
The hon. member for Athabaska mentioned also that our graduate students are in debt when they leave college. Supposing a student borrows $5,000; now, according to the new administrative criterions, if a student is given a loan of $5,000, it means that he was unable to find work during the summer or that his parents are not well-off. According to the program, he may have nine and a half years to pay back that $5,000. My figures are not necessarily correct, however it would mean that he could repay $43 a month on the capital and about $25 or $30 on the interest, which would amount to about $68 a month or $816 a year. In my opinion, our country is now going through a period of inflation. Wages are going up, and I do not think that $816 a year could really inconvenience a student once he has graduated. It could, for instance, inconvenience a student who would have to pay back that money while studying, but not once his studies are over.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the student loan program is to assist students to get an education. Once equipped, most of them are in a position to look after themselves. While I am not against the abolition of interest rates of this type, I believe the priority today should be in raising the ceiling of income which parents are allowed to earn before their children become disqualified from obtaining a student loan.
A number of people have discussed this aspect of the student loan program with me, telling me, as the case may be, that they had a son or a daughter turned down because the family income was in excess of the qualifying amount. At the same time, I sympathize with those parents, because their income was not really that much when one considers the responsibilities with which they were faced.
Many of the young people with whom I have spoken would look favourably upon there being an increase in the number of students who can qualify for a student loan by reason of a higher income ceiling which parents are allowed to earn. Their emphasis was on the importance of providing students with money while attending university. My strong feelings with regard to providing more funds for student loans under the federal-provincial agreement is conditioned by my own experience. Other hon. members have today mentioned students who are going through something of a state of depression because of their lack of funds while attending university. I am in full sympathy with the feelings of these people. This is why I am taking a very strong stand on increasing the amount of these loans. It is very depressing when a student sitting in a small room in a city a long way from home does not know where his next dollar is coming from.
Therefore I believe the emphasis today should be on the humanitarian aspect of educating our young people and producing the funds with which to educate them, because I believe they would be quite happy to look after themselves if they were provided with interest free loans during their university education and for six months afterwards.
Many favourable comments have been made here today about the abolition of university fees. This would of course help

immensely. But we must consider that a young person who borrows a great deal of money while attending university is faced with paying it back after completing his university education, at a time when he has to set up a new home and start a business career, with all the expense involved.
I think the day will come when we will abolish these interest rates. There is indeed considerable pressure for the abolition of university fees. If we remember our history, we will know that in Canada in the early days fees were payable even to attend many secondary schools. No one would think of doing this today.

speechtext:
I hope they do not get it for a long while.
I also wish to express my appreciation to the house leader for proposing that the three resolutions dealing with farm credit be considered almost concurrently. We are not asking that the rules be amended or suspended even temporarily, but certainly it is a fact that items Nos. 5, 6 and 7 on the order paper deal with farm credit, and the divisions between the various purposes of the acts following these resolutions is an arbitrary one. Indeed some of them overlap in many respects, and if the house accepts the amendments that I intend to propose, there will be even more overlapping of the acts.
I also wish to acknowledge the co-operation of the house leaders of the other parties in allowing us to proceed in this way with the discussion of the three resolutions.
The resolution in item No. 6 dealing with the Farm Credit Act which established the farm credit corporation and through it provides long term mortgage credit to Canadian farmers, is one of the most important government programs for the support and development of the agricultural industry.
I will not spend a lot of time on the background of these acts because I know that most hon. members, whether they were in this house prior to this parliament or not, are familiar with it, although I think a very brief explanation is in order so that the resolutions may appear in a more cohesive form.
The objectives of the program are to provide the capital to facilitate the organization of Canadian agriculture into viable farm units in the hands of our competent farmers so that
Farm Credit Act
agriculture may make the greatest possible contribution to the Canadian economy and provide farmers with equitable returns for their investment of capital, work and skills. It provides the opportunity for individual farmers, in consultation with credit advisers trained in farm organization and management and in farm financing, to obtain the capital required to reorganize, develop or expand their farm businesses, and thus is a most potent force in bringing about the adjustments and the rationalization in the use of farm land so essential to a viable agricultural industry.
Very briefly, it appears from statistics relating to the number of loans, that from the inception of the operations of the corporation in October 1959 until the end of March of this year, the corporation has made more than 72,000 loans for a total of more than one billion one hundred million dollars. About 50 per cent of these funds have gone toward assisting farmers to buy additional land to enlarge their farms. A very significant proportion has gone toward financing the construction of buildings and other improvements to farm land necessary for efficient production.
Between 1961 and 1966 the number of farms in Canada with gross sales in excess of $5,000 per annum increased from about 140,000 to about 192,000. In the same period the number of farms with gross sales of more than $10,000 per annum increased from 50,000 to 95,000 or 90 per cent. While there were many factors involved, there is no doubt that credit under the provisions of the Farm Credit Act made a very significant contribution to these adjustments. I also think that keeping agriculture efficient, not only in terms of cost but in terms of keeping an orderly flow of the raw material needed for our food industry moving into the stream, is also important to people other than farmers.
It is therefore important to emphasize that the beneficial results of a program of this nature accrue not only to the farming public but to the public at large in terms of the efficient and low cost production of food.
To keep pace with the rapid changes taking place in agriculture, there is a continuous need for adjustments in our farm credit program. Several of these adjustments are now being proposed. Further adjustments will be made in the light of and following the report of the agricultural task force which has been established to recommend guide lines for agricultural policy.

September 30, 1968
Farm Credit Act
As agriculture has developed, more and more farmers are arranging to conduct their farm businesses in co-operation with one another in various forms of partnerships, farming corporations or co-operative associations. It is important that these developments be recognized and that credit facilities be adjusted to meet the increased capital needs where two or more farmers wish to organize and operate their businesses together.
Another important amendment deals with Indians on Indian reserves. Indian farmers situated on reserves have so far been unable to borrow from the farm credit corporation because of their inability to mortgage their land. It would seem appropriate that the corporation be given authority to enter into appropriate agreements wth the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development so that appropriate arrangements can be made to provide credit for the development of viable farm businesses on Indian reserves.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Another important amendment that we will be proposing has to do with father and son business relationships. While the total number of farm operators is gradually decreasing, it remains essential for the future viability of the agricultural industry that there be a continuous flow of competent young men into agriculture. For this reason, it seems necessary, particularly in view of the increasing capital costs required to establish a viable farm business, to provide additional facilities to assist competent young men to get into this field. In particular, it seems desirable to adjust the provisions of the legislation so that a father who wishes to expand his farm business to bring in his son as a partner will be able to obtain the capital required to develop his farm to a size that will make it attractive for the son to join in the farm business. Amendments to this effect will be proposed.
When the Farm Credit Act was passed in 1959, the interest rate which the corporation might charge was fixed at 5 per cent. As we are all aware, interest rates in the general economy fluctuate from time to time. Any great differential between the rate at which the corporation lends money and the general level of interest rates will tend to distort the demand for credit from the corporation. In economists' terms, unrealistic interest rates tend to cause misallocation of resources, and in particular terms any savings as a result of a subsidized interest rate on capital borrowed for the purchase of land could make the cost

of the land excessively inflationary. For these reasons, it seems desirable, quite apart from the question of the subsidization of interest, to amend the Farm Credit Act so that rates can be established by the governor in council from time to time in relation to interest rates in the economy in general.
Turning to another aspect of this subject now, Mr. Chairman, I may say that at the moment the authorized capital of the Farm Credit Corporation is $40 million. On the basis of this capital, the corporation is authorized to borrow up to $1 billion, so that the total funds available to the corporation for lending amount to $1,040 million. On September 17, the total amount outstanding to the corporation on its commitments exceeded $1 billion. At the present rate of approval of loans to farmers, the total funds available to the corporation will be used up by the end of October or early November of this year. For this reason, it is essential that the authorized capital of the Farm Credit Corporation be increased in order to permit this lending program to continue. Of course, Mr. Chairman, I hardly need to add that amendments to provide for this will be proposed.
If I may, Mr. Chairman, I am now turning to the other resolutions, in compliance with the agreement we made earlier today. I should like to make a very brief explanation of some of the amendments that we intend to propose in respect of the Farm Machinery Syndicates Credit Act. This act was enacted in 1964 and lending commenced in January of 1965. Very briefly, the objective of this program is to provide a simple means whereby three or more farmers may co-operate in the purchase and use of farm machinery, thus saving overhead machinery costs. May I give a few statistics in relation to this act? From the inception of lending to the end of July of this year, 444 loans have been made to 346 syndicates for a total of about $3.7 million and for the purchase of about 1,388 machines of various types. Although the number of syndicates formed may not seem large, it is significant to know that some of the syndicates have found this operation so successful they have returned for second, third and even fourth loans to expand their co-operative use of farm machinery.
In the light of the experience to date, Mr. Chairman, there are several amendments to the program that now seem desirable. The present act requires the members of the syndicate to be farmers who are farming independently of each other. Experience shows that those farmers who co-operate in
September 30, 1968

the purchase and use of machinery tend to extend their co-operation to other aspects of their farming operations. For example, some of them may pool their land use to overcome problems relating to the timeliness of seeding and harvesting operations. As a result, they are no longer farming independently. For this reason, it seemed desirable to amend the legislation to that three or more farmers may borrow even though their operations may not be independent of one another in all the ways that the act now requires that word "independent" to be defined.
Some farmers have organized their co-operative efforts through the promotion of cooperative associations or corporations. At the moment, such farmers would be required to enter into separate syndicate agreements in respect of the use of machinery purchased through loans under the provisions of this act. We feel the terms of their association or incorporation already provide the basis upon which they might co-operate in the purchase and use of machinery. It seems unnecessary that they be required to enter into separate, new agreements in order to operate under the provisions of the act.
Much of the machinery and equipment which is most suitable for co-operative use by a group of farmers is of the type that requires installation in buildings designed for it. Examples of this would be equipment required for the washing, grading and packaging of fruits and vegetables, grain drying equipment and of course some types of production equipment. At the moment, the act provides only for the purchase of machinery. I believe it should provide also for the financing of the building site and the specially designed building required for the installation and proper use of this machinery or equipment. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, amendments will be proposed to incorporate these ideas.
To carry this a little further, there are buildings which may be profitably used cooperatively by a group of farmers in the various aspects of their farming operation. An example of this would be the efficient storage of fruits and vegetables which may require large, well equipped buildings beyond the needs or indeed the means of any one individual farmer. A group of farmers could profitably co-operate on the construction of storage facilities for products such as apples and potatoes. It would be possible to build a storage large enough to be economic and adequate for the needs of all.
Farm Credit Act
Another example is the hostel type of housing accommodation for seasonal labourers in areas where the type of crops being produced require an extensive amount of this kind of labour. We are all aware of the difficulties in obtaining seasonable labour for some types of produce. We recognize that one of the principal difficulties is the lack of housing accommodation for these workers. A group of farmers could co-operatively build the kind of housing accommodation required. For this reason, it is desirable to amend the provisions of this legislation to provide credit for the construction of buildings which groups of farmers might use co-operatively for this purpose in particular, but for other purposes as well.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take a great deal of time going through introductory remarks in connection with the other resolutions. There will be other opportunities. However, I should like to spend a few minutes now introducing resolution No. 5, which is the one that deals with the Farm Improvement Loans Act. The resolution indicates a number of amendments, Mr. Chairman, to the Farm Improvement Loans Act, which will reinstate this important farm credit facility in a way to permit it to serve the farming sector even more effectively than it did in the past.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Hon. members will require little by way of general introduction to this program, which is so well known. I must put on the record, however, a few statistics related to its history. It first came into effect in 1944 as a measure to encourage our chartered banks to make term credit readily available to farmers across the country, for a wide range of important projects, at reasonable cost. To this end the government guaranteed all loans made by the banks for purposes set out in the act. This guarantee has been renewed by parliament from time to time in respect of loans made during three year periods. The most recent period was added in September, 1964, to run from July 1, 1965 to June 30, 1968. Hon. members may recall that it did not prove possible to deal with this measure before the three year guarantee period expired on June 30, 1968. In view of the subsequent dissolution of the house, this is the first opportunity to bring this measure before the house for consideration.
Meanwhile, however, the Minister of Finance indicated publicly that it was his intention to seek amendments to the act as soon as

September 30, 1968
Farm Credit Act
possible to include another lending period and to make improvements in the legislation. As his predecessors had done previously under similar circumstances, the Minister of Finance advised the banks that when the legislation was introduced in the house the new lending period would be made retroactive to July 1 and that any loans they made after June 30 according to the terms and conditions now set out in the legislation would be covered by the government guarantee.
This act first came into effect nearly a quarter of a century ago to help make term credit more readily available to farmers on reasonable terms and conditions. As the Minister of Finance explained to the house when the measure was first introduced, the Farm Improvement Loans Act was designed as an incentive to banks to enter the term lending field to farmers on a major scale.
A maximum rate of interest of 5 per cent was included in the act, which rate at that time was sufficient to cover the banks' cost of operation and give them an incentive to go after the business. I think hon. members will agree that this legislation has been eminently successful in achieving its objective. The use that has been made of this facility over the years has shown considerable growth. Annual lending of about $10 million in 1946 rose to $100 million by 1960, and to the $200 million level by 1965. Since then, the growth has been slower.
