speechtext:
This indication of slower growth and decline in 1967 may have been explained in terms of developments affecting Canadian

agriculture generally; but subsequent developments suggest that it is a reflection of the increasing reluctance of banks to commit funds at 5 per cent, despite the presence of the government guarantee. During the latter part of last year and the early months of this year, when interest rates rose sharply, bank lending under the Farm Improvement Loans Act fell off sharply and virtually ceased some time before the lending period formally expired on June 30, 1968.
I mentioned a moment ago that this act was designed as an incentive for banks to make these loans, and I think it is important to keep in mind that the objective of this legislation is to facilitate the making of guaranteed loans to farmers; but the ultimate decision on whether such loans are made rests with the lender. Farm improvement loans are guaranteed by the government as to their repayment in the event of default, but the lenders are the source of financing. The lenders of these funds must, of course, take into account the prevailing general level of interest rates and the cost of them of their sources of funds.
An amendment to the act which makes the rate prescribable by regulations would enable the government to establish maximum rates that would be below rates that farmers would have to pay in the absence of the guarantee, but that would be high enough to enable the banks to continue to lend their wholehearted support to this program. It would also provide the flexibility necessary to see that the program continues on a fair and equitable basis to both borrower and lender by ensuring that the rates reflect changes over time in the general level of interest rates. Under these circumstances it should be possible for a new group of lenders to become active under this program.
The amendments I have just referred to would have the effect of reactivating operations under the act. I shall now turn to other amendments that would significantly broaden the operations under the act.
As hon. members are aware, the credit requirements of the farming sector for land purchases are now met almost in their entirety by the Farm Credit Corporation. With the rapidly growing credit requirements in recent years for both major and minor land purchases this has meant a growing demand on the government's cash resources. Of course, F.C.C. provides a good deal more than the funds to meet these credit requirements. There are many progressive and profitable farming enterprises in the country today
September 30, 1968

which became that way not only because they borrowed from the F.C.C., but also, and perhaps more so, because they received expert guidance and counsel from F.C.C.'s highly trained staff or agricultural experts. The F.C.C. has, however, financed in the past numerous smaller purchases of land not requiring the specialized service of the F.C.C. but capable of being suitably handled by regular commercial lenders. A case in point would be a relatively small piece of land that may come on the market and help a farmer round out his existing farm holdings. We are proposing to make such relatively minor land purchases eligible under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. For larger land purchases a farmer would of course continue to look to the F.C.C. for financing.
The addition of the purchase of land as an eligible loan purpose and the flexibility that is proposed on interest rates makes it appropriate to broaden the range of lenders among whom a farmer may wish to choose when making his financial arrangements. The proposed amendments would add as eligible lenders loan, trust and insurance companies, which are particularly familiar with mortgage lending, and credit unions and caisses populates, which could service their member-clients over the entire range of loan purposes under the act.
The inclusion of credit unions, which have a long and strong tradition in rural areas and particularly in western Canada will, I am sure, be welcome by those interested in rural co-operative movements.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
To accommodate this new loan purpose without unduly restricting a farmer's ability to borrow under the act for other purposes, such as the purchase of equipment, the amendments would raise the maximum loan amount that may be outstanding to a farmer at any one time to $25,000. An amount of up to $15,000 may be outstanding in respect of land purchases. The present loan limit of $15,000 for loan purposes, other than the purchase of land, would continue to apply, but both these loan limits would be made subject to a new over-all ceiling of $25,000. If a farmer wished, he could continue to borrow up to $15,000 for purposes covered in the present act, and have in addition up to $10,000 for the purchase of land. If he preferred to use up to $15,000 for the purchase of land, he would be able to obtain a government guaranteed loan up to $10,000 for other prescribed purposes.
Farm Credit Act
Mr. Chairman, I think we all recognize the importance of continuing what has so far been a very successful program. The proposed flexibility of interest rates, combined with the participation of new lenders, the addition of a new loan purpose and higher loan amounts, will no doubt provide the basis for a further successful period of credit support for farmers.
This is a brief outline of the amendments we intend to bring forward when the bills to follow these three resolutions are brought into the chamber. We have done the best we can, when framing these amendments, to make these three acts as useful and effective as possible. While they may not be perfect, I think they go a long way toward recognizing and making provision for needed development in agricultural credit requirements.
In conclusion I wish to thank all hon. members for the co-operation they have extended to me during the past few weeks. I know there are many problems in the field of agriculture and that these changes in farm credit legislation will not solve all of them. However, they will go some distance and we hope members in all parts of this house will co-operate with us in allowing us not only to deal with all the resolutions as a package, but to bring the subsequent bills forward one after the other; because I think the whole debate on these three bills deals essentially with one subject, that of farm credit, and it would be difficult to separate the three resolutions, or the three bills, and deal with them in the course of three separate debates.
The reinstatement, with improvements, of the Farm Improvement Loans Act is needed at once. Not a day goes by without a large number of letters passing over my desk from farmers who ask how quickly we can re-enact this piece of legislation. So it is needed right away. The need for the changes in the Farm Machinery Syndicates Act and the Farm Credit Act may not be so urgent, but we have committed all the money we are authorized to commit to the Farm Credit Corporation. So without making any attempt to restrict debate I would ask hon. members in all parts of the house to expedite the passage of these bills in order that we can make these services available to farmers.

Speaking on behalf of the Official Opposition I wish to express appreciation to the minister for his introduction of these three measures, so important to

Farm Credit Act
agriculture at the present time. I wish also to thank the hon. gentleman for giving us details of the amendments he proposes. They are many in number. We cannot hope to deal with all of them this evening, so the opposition reserves the right to consider them one at a time in later stages of the debate.
The hon. gentleman has pleaded with us tonight to pass these bills very quickly, telling us that the money is badly needed by the farm community. He certainly speaks the truth. But, Mr. Chairman, these funds have been needed, now, for many months by those engaged in agriculture. It would be interesting to see an evaluation of the hundreds of thousands of dollars spent by the farmers of this nation in higher interest rates because this government in its wisdom early last year declined to put this necessary legislation before the house.

speechtext:
The minister speaks of the 5 per cent interest rate. Under the Farm Improvement Loans Act the money is not available to farmers at the present time. The minister knows that for months this source of money has dried up, forcing farmers to pay interest rates of 13 per cent, 14 per cent and even more to the loan companies and the machinery companies in order to obtain new machinery or take advantage of the opportunity to improve their efficiency.
What we have before us tonight at long last is an admission by the government that agriculture needs more money, and a statement that interest rates will be permitted to rise in order to make this money available. We who sit on these benches intend to scrutinize the amendments very carefully. As far as farm improvement loans are concerned, and loans to machinery syndicates, we wish to make these available as quickly as possible, knowing how desperately they are needed.
May I suggest, since those two bills deal with short term loans, more or less, and since farm credit loans are a long term proposition, that the government seriously consider sending the latter piece of legislation to a reconstituted standing committee on agriculture, where an opportunity might be afforded of examining the procedure by which such loans are made, and the terms which might be

placed upon farmers. Every member of this house has encountered instances where farmers' applications for loans have been refused, on the ground that they are already operating economic units, and therefore do not need loans.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
At the same time other farm loans have been refused because farmers as yet do not have economic units and therefore cannot obtain them. As a result many farmers of this nation have found it almost impossible to comply with the regulations and obtain the necessary funds for expansion. So, Mr. Chairman, it is our earnest desire that the government give serious consideration to referring this one, of the three measures, to a standing committee, for an examination of the terms of the bill and the amendments proposed.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I would like to point out that the government does not solve any of the major farm problems by offering farmers an opportunity to get deeper in debt. In other words, Mr. Chairman, every farmer of this nation knows you cannot borrow yourself out of an economic obligation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBLE CLASSES, AMOUNT OF CAPITAL, INTEREST RATES, ETC.
speechtext: Not even the government can do that.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELIGIBLE CLASSES, AMOUNT OF CAPITAL, INTEREST RATES, ETC.
speechtext:
We found through the years that when extensive credit was available it has increased the cost of land, it has increased the cost of machinery and, according to the government's own statement, in the last six years it has put the farmers, through the farm credit bill alone, $1,100,000,000 further into debt.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I want to point out to the government that the farming community is going to look at these three bills with a great deal of suspicion, not because farmers do not want this money, not because they do not appreciate the increase in credit, but because they are going to be very suspicious of the open end where the government, at its discretion, may state what the rate of interest shall be, and at its discretion change the rate of interest.
In these bills I think we should have a definite formula, perhaps related to the present interest rate, in order that when they approach government for money farmers themselves will know definitely what they will be expected to pay this year, next year and any other year. So we must look at this part of the government's proposals with a great deal of suspicion and caution.
September 30, 1968

Further, Mr. Chairman, farmers today are going to be most hesitant in increasing their financial obligation, because during the last six years they have not been able to obtain any indication from the government as to where it thinks agriculture should go. There has been no policy, so much so that today a so-called efficient farm, as the government points out may, by the government's definition, be an inefficient farm tomorrow. This occurs, not through any fault of the operator, not through actual inefficiency of the operator, but because of changing trade patterns that are encouraged by the government, because of changing labour requirements that are encouraged by the government, because of a tremendous increase in imports being allowed by the government, and because of changes in tariff regulations which in themselves, taken singly or collectively, can reduce the gross returns of the most efficient farm, put it in a position of operational inefficiency and therefore, according to the government, place it in a position where it should pass out of existence.
Because of the substitute products coming on the market and because of overproduction in some segments of it, the dairy industry is in trouble. Every member of this house realizes that. Most dairy operators are of the considered opinion that in order to compete on an international basis they must be most proficient and efficient in their operation. With dairying, as it is today, some dairy farms will require $100,000 additional capital in order to modernize and take advantage of the most recent innovations. But dairy operators are sound businessmen and they are not going to borrow $100,000 unless they know the government's plans for the future of the industry.
We cannot have, as we had in the past under the previous government, three different national dairy proposals or plans in three years, with the result that dairymen had no idea what the government proposed for them. Businessmen are going to look at this very carefully before they tie up their funds for years in advance. The government tonight speaks of additional credit for farmers. We on this side say that farmers before they take advantage of this credit have a right to know what the government's policy is.
What has happened in the last three years to the farmers of this nation? The Ontario sugar beet industry passed out of existence. What about the farmers who took advantage of farm improvement loans to buy beet combines? They paid $3,000 or $4,000 for beet
Farm Credit Act
combines, but because of lack of a government sugar policy the beet industry went out of existence. How are those farmers expected to finance and pay for those machines?
What is happening to the corn industry today? Hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of farm equipment is tied up in it. Hundreds of thousands of dollars of Farm Credit Corporation money is tied up in enlarging com farms. What is going to happen if this commodity passes out of existence, due to the economic climate? How are those farmers going to repay their loans?
What is going to happen to the canning industry if we allow, as we have done, imports to come into this country to such a degree that that industry and those engaged in it are on a marginal economic existence? What happens if we cannot sell our wheat? Who is going to repay these loans totalling $1,100,000,000 that farmers have borrowed since 1961? If the the farm industry collapses who is going to repay this money?
What is going to happen to our beef industry if we increase imports of beef from Agen-tina and other countries? What is going to happen to the tomato industry if we continue to import tomatoes from Mexico, Bulgaria and Portugal? These, Mr. Chairman, are the questions farmers are asking. Where do we go from here?

speechtext:
Farmers realize, but the government does not, that under present policies the farming industry can no longer exist as a great industry in Canada. They do not need a task force to tell them what the problem is: They know what the problem is. The problem is that they are no longer governed by the law of supply and demand, or the law of a free enterprise system. They know that as little, local, provincial co-operatives they cannot hope to deal efficiently and effectively with state controlled sales and state controlled subsidies. They know that as individual farmers, as co-operative farmers or as provincial organizations they cannot compete with managed markets. They cannot compete with international food chains that can buy all over the world, and through their own distribution systems take advantage of vast markets.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
The fanners turn to the federal government for this. They want to know what the federal government intends doing about it, and

September 30, 1968
Farm Credit Act
whether that government will provide them with the domestic market. They wish to know whether we are to have our own Canadian market, or whether the government intends as in the past to encourage imports in a desperate last ditch attempt to force down the cost of living. Is the farming community to be sacrificed for this? Are the farmers to be asked to bear the brunt of the new taxation measures the government proposes? What will happen to the farming community under the new GATT trading arrangements and the Kennedy round? This has never been discussed in the house. The government has not stated its policy in this regard. Certainly it has indicated that some industries will be hurt and that an attempt will be made to compensate those industries, but where does the farming community fit into all this? Many times when a farming industry is not hurt directly, if some of the allied industries are hurt it is the farmers who pay.
The minister tonight has stated that there is an attempt to increase the credit to the farmers of this nation. I compliment the government on this and on some of the amendments which I believe will help the situation. I should like to point out, however, one example. Under the syndicates act accommodation is to be provided for seasonal labour. In other words, if a group of farmers wishes to employ seasonal labour to harvest the crop in season, be it strawberries, tomatoes, apples, tobacco or some other crop, under the terms of the act, as I understand it, the government will be prepared to lend the money necessary to construct the accommodation. What will happen if this labour is imported from Jamaica, and the immigration policy changes? What will happen if the local canning company to which this produce is delivered is put out of business because of imports? W11 this group of farmers, which can no longer engage profitably in this endeavour, be forced either into bankruptcy or into paying off these loans?
I suggest that through the extension of credit alone we can neither answer nor hope to answer the many serious problems facing agriculture today. The farmers of this nation who have been waiting impatiently for years are now told that when the task force makes its report the government will consider the recommendations. It is no wonder the farmers of this nation are impatient. They know what the problems are, and they expect government action to solve some of these problems.
[Mr. Danforth.l
They expect the government to act on their behalf. Farm credit alone will not suffice.
Recently we have seen what can happen with regard to a commodity, and I am speaking once more of corn. In a single year we have reached the point where, at the present time, the receipts for this crop are considered to be lower than the cost of production. We have seen what has happened in the case of sugar beets. Farmers who for years considered this to be their main crop suddenly found that they could not grow it any longer. We have seen what has happened to the small canning companies across this nation when they have been faced in the marketplace with sudden imports.
We have seen what can happen with regard to credit. Farmers who have depended on the Farm Credit Corporation or the Farm Improvement Loans Act to help them in time of need have found, through government action, that this source of credit has been taken away from them. When they have needed a loan, they have attempted for months to survive without it. We are about to see what may happen under the changing trade patterns brought about by the Kennedy round.
I do not wish to appear to be pessimistic, but under the changing regulations in respect of the dumping duties, and the trading which has been taking place on a commodity basis, I fear there are some segments of the Canadian agricultural industry which will be in dire circumstances. Therefore I say to you, Mr. Chairman, and through you to the government, that we intend to do all we can in an attempt to get this legislation through the house as quickly as possible. But we will do our very best to see that the interests of the farmers of this nation are taken care of, because it is long past the time when members in this house should be awakened and made aware of the circumstances faced by the agricultural community today. They should begin, in a constructive manner, to do something about it. We cannot introduce this legislation, but when the legislation comes before the members of this house we intend to do our very best to serve the farmers of this nation.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when speaking for our group with regard to this credit program that is being offered to the agricultural industry as a whole, I must say that I believe some real opportunity to do something new and imaginative may well have been missed. While I say this, I am aware that the minister
September 30, 1968

knows I have a considerable respect for his ability, since we have known one another for a number of years. When one looks at this program he must consider that although the intention is that more money will be made available to farmers in the form of credit, it is proposed that this money be made available to them-I think we must assume-at a much increased rate of interest. The term used was that the present rates are unrealistic. I suppose therefore that we will have some realistic rate, and this will depend on what particular economist we are listening to at what particular time.
Are these interest rates to be realistic in terms of the farmers' costs of production? This remains to be seen. Before I talk about interest rates, however, I should like to say that what is lacking here more than anything else is a co-ordinated approach to farm credit in an attempt to tie together the long term, intermediate and short term credit. Certainly a very high percentage of farmers are now using these three types of credit.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
What we are being offered here is just a continuation of what we have had. The proposals in respect of the Farm Improvement Loans Act are just the same, with some added money made available. The Farm Credit Corporation will continue to operate as it has. There is no method of tying these together so as to have a package approach. In that way the whole scope of the farming community could be served.
Back in November of 1962 a working paper was prepared for the royal commission on banking and finance by D. W. Carr and Associates. This working paper was in respect of farm credit in Canada. As far back as that date Mr. Carr and his associates made some recommendations on this very subject. The report said:
The most important lenders in short and intermediate term farm credit were the chartered banks. A significant part of this lending was under the Farm Improvement Loans Act through which a degree of public responsibility for such farm credit had been initiated. To carry out these responsibilities effectively and most profitably the banks operations under F.I.L.A. clearly needed the specialized technical guidance and advice of agricultural credit experts. The interest of both the banks and the farmers would be best served by F.I.L.A. having closer association with the federal Department of Agriculture. This could enable F.I.L.A. lending to be expanded with the confidence that the risks were minimized by sounder lending techniques for both F.I.L.A. and ordinary farm loans and should thus reduce the risk on the banks' ordinary farm loans also.
29180-39}
Farm Credit Act
Instead of following this line and looking for more advice we are going to open up this field to the insurance and trust companies, and the government is going to guarantee them against loss. This means that if, as a previous speaker has suggested, a farmer gets in over his head, the farmer himself is taking the risk. There is always a risk when you lend money but it can be minimized, and this is one way it could have been done. The report then continues indicating that a coordinating body should be set up to co-ordinate the various lending agencies and states:
A most important function of this development co-ordination body would be to establish in the beginning more adequate sources of information for appraising trends and developments in farm financing, to initiate research and analytical appraisals of changes and problems in farm credit demand and in its sources of supply, to develop and promote the use of improved techniques by both private and public lenders and to review and develop measures to meet the changing needs in credit services to farmers.
This information has been available to the government since 1962 and the government paid good hard cash to get it, yet it has not been used. What the report is saying in effect is that more should be done in the way of what is being done by the Farm Credit Corporation. The Farm Credit Corporation has an electronic farm accounting program which is now serving 2,700 Canadian farmers, providing them with information which is important to their day by day decisions and long term planning. The Farm Credit Corporation states that farmers use this service for a wide range of purposes in the size and operation of farms and so on. The report states that this information is important to the development of lending methods to meet the changing needs of farm financing in Canada. The corporation's success with this electronic farm accounting program has been a contributing factor in the general interest in developing a national farm recordkeeping program. The corporation's experience has been made available to those involved in developing such a national program.
I hope this information will be used. This is the type of thing that should be tied in with other lending programs. If we allow the banks and trust companies to enter the short and intermediate term lending field, without any safeguards and without having any cross reference information, in a certain number of years we will look around and see that some of these loans have become bad loans. But no one will have the precise information which would indicate the reason for such a situation.

September 30, 1968
Farm Credit Act
It is in this direction that I suggest our farm credit policy should be headed. I see no indication in the resolutions now before us or in the remarks by the Minister of Agriculture that there is any concept on the government side which recognizes this need. We have a real opportunity in this lending field to obtain information and working knowledge of what is happening, but we have never taken advantage of that opportunity.
The Farm Credit Corporation has made some advances over the years and is doing a better job than the old farm loans board, its predecessor. It is gathering information and giving more guidance and counselling to the farmer, although to my knowledge it has not yet built up the specialized staff of supervisors that should be available. Perhaps this is government policy.
The Carr report finally states:
The most effective way of initiating this development agency would be to establish a public body probably attached to the Department of Agriculture to co-ordinate these various development activities. The established governmental agencies for direct farm credit could be fitted into it to fill their role as a part of the over-all credit system developed under this body and continuing to supply the important services they had established. Thus the Farm Credit Corporation could maintain its mortgage services supplemented by the new facilities as they were developed by the co-ordinating body.
This working paper concludes by stating:
-progressive improvements in farm credit services in Canada could be expected, the path of agricultural adjustment would be made smoother and less difficult for farmers and the competitive position of Canadian agriculture would be strengthened.
Whether this would happen or not I do not know, but this is a what the fifth annual report of the Economic Council suggested we should be aiming for; and credit should be part of the policy followed to reach these objectives. We are not going to meet these objectives as a result of what has been submitted to us. I suggest with all sincerity that the Minister of Agriculture should be concerned about this situation and should consider these suggestions.
I have no particular objection to the trust companies and insurance companies getting into the lending field. I suppose that in a free enterprise economy, which hon. members on the other side of the house support, it is up to those companies to decide. However, on looking back at what they have done for farmers, I am wondering just how much good such a policy will do for agricultural communities. When one looks at the long term record, he
IMr. Gleave.l
sees that these companies have done very little. Perhaps for their own reasons at this time they want a piece of this action.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
The risks of agriculture are there, and they are big risks. Those of us in the business know how big they are. The government will be doing the farmers of Canada no favour if they increase the credit risks in farming. The previous speaker outlined at some length the situation in agriculture and farming. I realize the situation as well as he does, but I do not want to take up a great deal of time telling the government what I assume they surely know, that agriculture and farming is not one of the industries that will carry an 8 per cent and 9 per cent interest rate.
Surely they know that. But they come to this house with resolutions which say, in effect, "We are not going to leave it to parliament any more to set the interest rates for the Farm Credit Corporation. We are not going to leave it to parliament to set the interest rates under the Farm Improvement Loans Act." Apparently they do not think parliament has the good, common sense to do this, although parliament has done it since the inception of these measures.
The government says, "We will not leave that with you. We want you to write us a blank cheque, and in our good, reasonable and wise time we will set some realistic interest rates." Have they so little confidence in the economy that they feel they cannot bring before parliament a level of interest rates that will survive for three years; or are they afraid that if they alter the interest rates which now exist in an economy in which we are trying to live, parliament will not accept the interest rates they will have to propose? Are they unwilling to say to the people of Canada that farming in this country is in such a situation, and the earning margins are so low, that if we want farmers to stay in business we have to subsidize the interest rates as they exist in Canada? These are the circumstances which exist; the previous speaker did not exaggerate.
From the papers I have before me I could quote the president of the Dairy Council of Canada, who said we used to get one-fifth of a cent margin on a quart of milk, but many farmers are not now receiving this margin. You can open the books in Saskatchewan on the farm management study that has been carried out by farm clubs and the provincial department of agriculture, and the story is
September 30, 1968

there for you to read. You can go to Manitoba and get the same kind of information. The story is there to be read. We do not have to guess any more in connection with many of these things.
Therefore I say that this parliament should not accept the suggestion in these resolutions that the interest rate be left to the tender mercies of the government. I say this is a proper decision for this house to make. Whatever interest rates are proposed, they should be put into the act and brought before this house.
To realize the problems which exist in agriculture one has only to read some of the briefs from farm organizations. I have here a brief from the National Farmers Union. This is one matter on which the National Farmers Union and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture do not diverge to any great extent. The submission of the National Farmers Union says, in regards to credit:
What is important is security of tenure, and this, in our view, can best be provided by realistic public policies and participation combined with a social concept on the type of rural community our nation should be aiming for in the future. The Farm Credit Corporation is now a useful instrument, but is too restrictive in its lending policies, requiring, as it does, unreasonable security on its loans. For example, in a recent case, a farm wife in Saskatchewan was required to sign away her rights under the provincial homestead act on the home quarter section of land which, in addition to two other quarter sections of land, was required by F.C.C. as collateral for a loan of $12,000 for the construction of a farm home.
I wonder whether the trust companies and insurance companies will be more generous when they become a part of the credit program. I have my doubts. Let me quote from the Union Farmer:
-J. B. Hansen, Royal Bank supervisor, who will be in charge of the bank's revamped agricultural headquarters. At the same time it was announced that the bank, realizing that farming today is big business, has appointed representatives in the prairie provinces who are "experts" and will advise on agricultural questions.
I have no objection to the bank appointing experts to advise on agricultural questions. If they think they are to lend a great deal of money, they will probably need experts. But this proves the point I put forward at the beginning of my remarks, that if the job was being properly done within the Department of Agriculture, the bank could turn to the trained men in the lending department of the Department of Agriculture and say, "We are willing to be part of the program. We are willing to lend the money. What are the
Farm Credit Act
facts?" Do we want each bank employing a bunch of experts, for whom we are all going to pay? With regard to the Farm Credit Corporation, the trust companies and insurance companies, is each one going to build up his own little gathering of experts, so-called?
One thing about the farmer is that he never runs out of experts. I am always amazed at the number of people who are sure they know how to run his business better than he does. I have set out some of the things that I think are relevant to these three resolutions, and with that I leave it to the minister responsible.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am happy, in the name of the members of the Ralliement Creditiste, to answer and to comment upon the very interesting speech made a few moments ago by the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) concerning the three resolutions intended to extend farm credit.
Mr. Chairman, in an article published in the Financial Post on January 29, 1966, Mr. John Schryner said this:
The transfer of agricultural property to the new generation has created a great demand for farm credit. This transfer began early in the 1960s and, according to some economists, will continue during the 1970s before declining gradually.
I am very pleased with this statement by Mr. Schryner and also with some of those made by the hon. Minister of Agriculture in his speech a few moments ago. The minister announced that he would introduce measures intended to encourage young people to take possession of their land and to continue their parents' work. ..
Mr. Chairman, we know that the problem of young farmers is enormous. We must, therefore, encourage them to show a greater interest in agricultural matters and, to do that, we must take steps to help them become integrated in that sector.
I would like, therefore, to tell the Minister of Agriculture, who is here tonight and has delivered an eloquent speech, that I thank him for the particulars he gave us and I hope he will take further steps to help young people to become integrated in the agricultural sector.
Mr. Chairman, today is a time of reflection for eastern and western farmers alike. It is a time of reflection or meditation, if you like, because if there is one group which is serious, it is the farming community.
The farming community has always been the quietest. As mentioned recently by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert), it has always been the one that worked when it was asked to, that produced when it was asked to, and which remained silent when it was told: Produce and keep quiet.
Mr. Chairman, the farm people as a group have given a lot in the past, they have never refused to produce. But today the farmer is asking himself: Why bother to keep up production when my products are selling at a loss? That is a serious problem, Mr. Chairman, and I hope that the Minister of Agriculture will take note thereof.

It has often been said that the production problem has been settled once for all. As a former Social Crediter-I doubt that he still is-the minister is well aware of it. Production in itself can easily meet Canadian needs. As far as the consumer is concerned, his purchasing power is inadequate to buy and sell that production. The problem is there, Mr. Chairman. When one says that Canada is a rich country, one means that it is rich in possibilities, rich in resources, rich in its future, rich in goodwill, rich in hopes and, for the Canadian farmer, it is rich in disappointments.
We now have in Canada a floundering farming industry. How come? Because each time a farmer could hope to get some kind of assistance, a loan from the Farm Credit Corporation for instance, the same silent thief is always there to prevent the farmer from improving his lot and I refer to the rate of interest. The rate of interest, the so-called silent thief, is protected by all governments, either Liberal or Conservative.
Mr. Chairman-and I will be brief-in 1955, the consumer price index rose to 112.1, as against 100 in 1949. In 1964, the same index reached 132.4 and I did not obtain yet the figures for 1968, since the minister took us by surprise. But nevertheless, the consumer price index has shot up once more.
And, during the same time, has the farmer's profit increased? I ask the minister: During the time when the consumer price index was continually rising, did the net profit of Canadian farmers, the western or eastern farmers, increase proportionately to the cost of living?
I know the minister is sincere enough to answer: No.
Mr. Chairman, that is the core of the problem. First of all, we must adapt our modern needs to a modern economy. Let us look at the scandal prevailing in the field of agriculture.
In the past, the Bois-Francs farmers received about two and a half cents a pound, but this year the crop was amazing. Due to this surplus production, potatoes only yielded one and a half cents a pound with the result that several farmers are on the brink of bankruptcy.

In my province alone the sale of farm equipment has declined to such an extent that many dealers have been forced into bankruptcy. One wholesale firm in a three month period reports 18 failures in its list of dealers. This is one result of the inconvenience caused to farmers who were unable to finance replacement equipment, needed especially because of adverse weather experienced during planting, cultivating and harvesting seasons.
I welcome the renewal of the Farm Improvement Loans Act, but I question some of its clauses. It seems to me that the cabinet of this country is taking on a job for itself that is completely unnecessary. I see no point whatever in having interest rates left to the cabinet to decide, in their wisdom. This prerogative is completely unnecessary. In my view it is further evidence that this government wishes to extend its tentacles into every phase of life of the Canadian people. There may be an exception as far as the bedrooms of the nation are concerned, but this unilateral setting of the interest rate is really none of the cabinet's business. Surely the government can negotiate with the financial institutions of this country and come up with a permanent rate. Let it be a fluctuating rate, if you like, but let it be established through a publicized formula.
Experience over the years has shown that the farm improvement loan has not been abused. The loss ratio in relation to the amount lent has been minimal and I suggest that a formula along the lines I have suggested could be worked out. For example, most financial firms and banks know what their overhead is. They know their costs of administration and we know the loss ratio. Why, therefore, can a formula not be worked out based on the prime lending rate of banks and other financial institutions, plus an agreed surcharge. I do not know what the surcharge might amount to; I am sure the banks would tell us. If one bank wanted 1 per cent and another needed only three quarters of one per cent we might even see a little competition entering the business.

I agree particularly with the concept of broadening the classes of persons eligible. Probably there is more justification here for the cabinet to set interest rates than there is in the case of farm improvement loans. Under the Farm Credit Act government money goes out; under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, bank money is lent under a minimal government guarantee. I say there is no need to change the interest rate under which moneys will be lent under the Farm Credit Act. The present high interest rates will not always stay in effect.

Some in this youthful cabinet are old enough to remember that we did not always have these high interest rates. Less than 30 years ago people with money to invest were happy to buy government bonds yielding 3 per cent. Who is to say that with farm credit loans running for upwards of 30 years interest rates will not come down drastically long before those loans are paid off. Over the past 100 years the money market has shown a remarkable history of ups and downs. Some economists go so far as to predict when these cycles will take place. For my purpose this evening it is sufficient to mention what has happened in the past 50 years.
From 1919 to 1929 long term Canadian dollar bonds gave an annual average yield of 5.07 per cent. From 1929 to 1939 the average yield was 3.88 per cent. From 1939 to 1949 the average yield was 2.93 per cent, and from 1949 to 1959 that average yield was 3.67 per cent. What the average for this decade will be is anyone's guess. Most decidely the average yield will be up. Certainly the rate will be as high as or higher than any we have seen in this century. Nevertheless, Mr. Chairman, these trends were evident a century ago, and before that. There is nothing new about them.
I therefore urge the government to keep at 5 per cent the lending rate on moneys lent under the Farm Credit Act. If necessary, the government ought to put government money into the corporation administering the act. If it does that it will have a credit mark opposite its record, a mark which will show that the government, in one instance, tried to keep our agricultural industry alive.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
I say again that these high interest rates will not last forever, and the burden on the treasury would be small in relation to the long term good which could be accomplished. Probably before many years have passed, before many of these liabilities are paid off, interest rates will once again be down. The inflationary effect of subsidized interest rates which the minister mentioned will not, in practice, have much of an impact. In my view the cabinet would do well to spend more of its time maintaining a climate in which our farmers could sell their products at a reasonable price. I suggest it would be far more profitable for them to spend their time on this, rather than sit around setting interest rates.

maintopic: HARBOURS-ROBERTS BANK, B.C.-CONSTITUTIONAL JURISDICTION RESPECTING RAILWAY LINE
HARBOURS-ROBERTS BANK, B.C.-CONSTITUTIONAL JURISDICTION RESPECTING RAILWAY LINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a week ago today I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) the following question, as recorded at page 326 of Hansard:
In view of the situation of continuing conflict concerning British Columbia Hydro's rail route to Roberts Bank, and in view of the fact that the provincial government controls a sole and vital link between two federal facilities, the port and the national railway system, what action does the federal government intend to take in regard to the problem of constitutional jurisdiction that is involved?
It would be almost possible, Mr. Speaker, to overestimate the amount of concern that this matter is causing among citizens of the lower mainland of B.C. As a matter of fact, my colleagues in this party have been trying unsuccessfully to get an answer to this question ever since we came down here. My colleague from Vancouver East was the latest to try this afternoon to get some ministerial statement on the matter.
The British Columbia cabinet has authorized the B.C. Hydro and Power Authority to build, or in part to rebuild 17 miles of track which would form part of an access rail line to Roberts Bank in the Matsqui area in order that initially shipments of coal from the Crowsnest area can be made to the new super port.
The reason that public opinion in the lower mainland area is so upset is that the provincial government has completely ignored the recommendations of the Lower Mainland Regional Planning Board which, along with


its 28 member municipalities, was given by this same provincial government the responsibility of land use planning and zoning for the whole lower mainland area.
The planning board strongly recommended an alternative rail route to provide service to Roberts Bank via the existing Fraser river industrial and railway corridor. The board warns that the B.C. Hydro route jeopardizes the future of the people of the lower mainland, of half the population of British Columbia. It advises that this new rail traffic would create additional major hazards of accident, air and soil pollution, would cause further noise intrusion, and would damage the appearance of the countryside completely unnecessarily. Land values in the immediate vicinity of the railway would go down and municipal tax revenues decrease as a result.
Most serious of all, the B.C. Hydro route would spell the destruction of the Boundary Bay area with its unparalleled recreation potential and its natural beauty on a magnificent scale. With this would go the destruction of one of the few remaining wildlife sanctuaries that exist in southern B.C.
No wonder that the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose), who represents a part of this whole area, declares that the proposed location of the railway defies every tenet of enlightened land use planning and reduces the Lower Mainland Regional Planning Board to complete irrelevance. I believe that all members in this house from British Columbia share this view.
From the standpoint of the federal interest much is involved. A super port is to be built at Roberts Bank and the control of the port is clearly within federal jurisdiction. Equally clear is the need for the federal authority to have undisputed access to the port.
The provincially controlled B.C. Hydro railway line to Roberts Bank would be connected with the interprovincial rail lines of Canada, which again are clearly under federal jurisdiction. Surely this situation presents a constitutional problem for the federal government, one that calls for immediate consultation with the provincial authorities, and one that certainly cannot be dodged, at least any longer.
The fact that two federal cabinet ministers seem to have differing opinions about the degree of federal jurisdiction in this matter- they have made no secret of their differences, at least judging from speeches they have made in B.C.-merely points up the need for a speedy and decisive solution. They both
September 30, 1968	COMMONS
cannot be right. This matter is either under B.C. provincial jurisdiction, or federal jurisdiction.
Quite apart from the problem of federal access to the Roberts Bank port, but very relevant to the problem, is the federal government's interest in regional planning and the conservation and development of Canada's natural resources, both from the standpoint of productivity and of human environment.
In a matter of such great significance to our province and indeed to the whole of this country I submit that the federal government owes the members of this house, the people of British Columbia and all the people of Canada an explanation on this point. I believe we should have a statement concerning the government's intentions. I honestly believe that the federal government is no longer in a position to evade this matter, and leave it to the provincial government to hold the whip hand in respect of this Roberts Bank situation.

maintopic: UNITED NATIONS-BIAFRA-FAILURE TO BRING MATTER BEFORE GENERAL ASSEMBLY
UNITED NATIONS-BIAFRA-FAILURE TO BRING MATTER BEFORE GENERAL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question I asked this afternoon and did not quite succeed in fielding dealt with a matter of great importance. The people of Canada are asking what is being done about the Biafra situation, and they are asking particularly why the United Nations is not dealing with the matter in some way.
I note that the minister referred to the danger of divisive action if this matter were dealt with in general terms, and I noticed that the Secretary General used similar phraseology. I want again in passing to note that the United Nations does deal with a good many divisive items and it would be somewhat unrealistic to confine the attention of the United Nations only to those questions on which there was harmony.
Surely in a matter of burning concern and deep anxiety to our people, and to thoughtful, sensitive people throughout the world, we should not be fearful of lack of unanimous support for the suggestions we might make. It is my contention that the question should have been on the provisional agenda of the General Assembly long ago. If the government had thought it wise, it could have been directed to one of the non-political committees, and the second and third committees come into my mind immediately. At this juncture I would agree that the Security Council is not the avenue for discussion at this time.
The UN does not deal only with political questions. There is a wide range of interests and debate, as anybody who has been there knows. The field is literally the world, and the agenda is immense. This session the General Assembly has 90 items on the provisional agenda. Surely it is not a cardinal point in Canada's foreign policies that we must be universally loved and have unanimous support for our eternal endeavours. If any effort to have the UN general assembly deal with

DEBATES	Sepiember 30, 1968
the humanitarian aspects of the Biafra situation, with the starvation and suffering of thousands of people, should put us in a minority position in the assembly-and this seems to be part of the government's thinking-then I say that on such an issue this would be an honoured position and a noble posture for this country to be in.
While the minister knows, I am not sure that the public know the procedure in respect of the General Assembly agenda. It is not as difficult as we have been led to believe. Rule 13 of the rules and procedures of the General Assembly lists the ways in which the provisional agenda is formed and what it shall include. Rule 13(e) says that the provisional agenda of the regular session shall include all items proposed by any member of the United Nations. Had this item been proposed any time during the summer, when the government had this matter very much in mind, as we were told, the UN could have been seized of it at any time, and thus this technical hurdle would have been overcome. Hopefully, had the whole situation been resolved by the O.A.U.,-and that would have been a lot to expect,-there would be no great difficulty in the United Nations dropping that item from the agenda.
Nor is it terribly difficult to recall situations where items are not in fact reached. In other words, the fact that the question may have been dealt with in another milieu was no excuse for the delegation of Canada not having this item placed upon the General Assembly agenda. Thus could the General Assembly mobilize world opinion to ameliorate the suffering of the Biafrans.
I note that the secretary general in his letter mentions insufficient financial support as a reason for the failure of voluntary organizations to bring about the amount of relief required to the population suffering in Biafra. Of course he is right. But the General Assembly, surely, would be the forum in which world interest could be stimulated and a measure of world relief and sacrifice, in financial terms, could be encouraged.
It is regrettable that among all the items in the 90-item agenda, this is not included. There are so many ways in which an item could have been constructed. I see here item No. 45: Multilateral food aid. Item No. 46 is: Increase in the production and use of edible protein. There are many, many items which are not political items and would not raise the spectre of these divisive repercussions which have been mentioned. But alas, that
September 30, 1968

has not been done. It should have been done. I do not think the government should raise the great curtain of impenetrable difficulty in having the UN seized of the matter.
It is regrettable that the opportunity was missed and I hope the minister and the government will make every effort to compensate for their failure to take action when action was easier than it may be now. We wish them well in whatever action they may feel it incumbent to take.

I wish to tell you also of my deep appreciation for your references to my statements regarding the distressing fratricidal strife in Nigeria, and X am greatly encouraged by your support of the position which I have taken concerning this situation. I agree with you that raising the situation in Nigeria in general terms before the United Nations General Assembly could be divisive, particularly in light of the resolutions adopted by the last two meetings of the Assembly of Heads of State and Government of the Organization of African Unity in Kinshasa and Algiers, respectively.
If the government felt that it would be possible to add one little bit to the amount of aid that would get through to the starving people in Nigeria-Biafra by raising this question in the United Nations, we would be glad to do so. We would do this if we felt that by raising the questions in the United Nations
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion we could in any way contribute to the relief of the suffering that is going on in Nigeria-Biafra.
We found, however, on exploring the situation that the countries which shared our concern believed that all that would happen- and I had to agree with them-was that there would be a political debate about the future of Nigeria, and that this would lead not to an increase in the amount of aid but to a kind of divisive, political debate that would actually detract from the aid that might otherwise be going to these suffering people.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
This was our view and, as you will see from the letter that I have read from the Secretary General, it was his view. I have no reason to question that judgment. However, I would add that it is my view and the view of the government that we should be working for the establishment of some kinds of procedures in the future when situations like this arise again, when there is an acknowledged method of dealing with these humanitarian concerns, by establishing rules that receive international agreement, and establishing agencies that are unquestioned when they want to supply aid to the innocent victims of a civil war such as this one. It seems to me that this is how we should be concentrating our efforts now. It is quite clear from what the Secretary General has said, and from our explorations, that to raise this question now would only raise the political issues which would detract from it, and would not aid the suffering people.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 10.25 p.m.

September 30, 1968
